metadata.tagline: You start out wanting the right name on the master's killer before the road carries a cart and the house hands the magistrate the nephew.
metadata.rating_advisory: Recommended for teen readers (13+). Contains a non-graphic murder investigation, threat of wrongful conviction, and themes of social coercion, blackmail, and ruined reputations.

intro.text: You are the new housekeeper, a fortnight in post, addressed by your surname and expected not to be noticed; last night you did your rounds with a candle and a ring of keys while the master's seven guests moved about the house, and this morning the master is dead behind his study door and you are the only person who knows where each of them was and when. You came here a widow from a smaller house, hired by the master himself, who told you on your first morning that he meant to put his house in order before Christmas; you have not yet been given the study key, because he kept the only one on his own chain.

description.text: There is plaster dust down the front of your black, from standing too near when the study door came down, and you have not yet been given leave to go and brush it off.
Your apron pockets are heavy and do not hang straight; anyone who looked would see a housekeeper carrying more than her keys. No one looks.
You have taken the cap off and put it back on twice. Your hands are steady; it is your mouth you do not trust, the shape it makes before you have decided what it will say.

You have been up and down the back stairs so often this morning that your hem is wet from the yard and you smell of tallow and snow. Your face, in the hall glass, is a servant's face: closed, correct, and waiting.
Black stuff dress, white cap, a fortnight's worth of this house's cold in your shoulders. You look like what you are meant to be: a woman nobody need remember was in the room.

says.text: A fortnight. Long enough to know which boards speak and which bells are out of true; not long enough for anyone upstairs to have learned your Christian name. That is what makes you useful now, and what makes you nothing: a stranger's word is a stranger's word, and a servant's is a servant's, and you are both.

He hired you himself, which is not how it is done, and said on your first morning that he meant to have the house in order by Christmas. You took it for a remark about the linen. You are no longer sure it was. You came here from a smaller house with a character and a ring on a ribbon, and you have been careful since to be exactly as much as was wanted and no more.

He has begun to say 'Mrs Vane' as if it were a name and not a correction. Forty years in this house and he has told you, in his way, that you are not the enemy. It would be easier if he had not; you saw his candle on the back stairs at a quarter past ten, and it was not lighting his own way.

He has not forgiven the master for hiring you, and he will not forgive you for being hired. Every word you say today he will weigh as a stranger's. But he lit someone up the back stairs last night, and whatever he thinks of you, you both know you saw it.

Forty years in the master's service, and a fortnight of yours over his head. He is correct to you in every particular, which is how a man of his sort says what he thinks. You do not dislike him. You think he loved the master, in the way a man loves a house, and that he would rather the house kept its secret than that you told it.

He listens when you speak, which no one else upstairs has done, and he calls your account 'evidence' as though it were a thing with weight. It is a flattering word. You notice it is always your evidence for his case that he wants read aloud, and never the parts that do not fit.

He has stopped asking what you saw and begun telling you what you saw. 'You will have noticed, Vane—' and then the thing he needs. A magistrate would take his word before yours without troubling to hear yours. He knows it. He is deciding whether you do.

The master's oldest friend, and since the door came down the nearest thing the house has to a master. He gives orders well. He wants your timeline, in your own voice, in the drawing room, and he has not yet said in support of what. You would like to be sure he is grieving before you give it to him.

He has begun to carry himself like the heir, and to speak to you as the heir speaks to a housekeeper: pleasantly, from a height. If the old will stands he is your master by Christmas. You saw him come down the back stairs at twenty to eleven and cross the yard to the stables in his shirt-sleeves, in the snow, and he does not yet know that you did.

He is frightened, and a frightened young gentleman is a dangerous thing to be the only witness against. He has looked at you twice this morning as if trying to remember whether you were in the passage. You were. Whether what you saw hangs him or clears him you have not yet worked out, and you suspect neither has he.

Twenty to eleven, the back stairs, the yard, the stables. You know it to the minute because the kitchen clock struck the half and you had counted the doors since. It may be the thing that convicts him. It may be the thing that saves him. It is, either way, the only thing in this house that is yours.

She has found her composure again and wears it like the pearls. 'One woman to another,' she said, and it was a kindness and a hook at once. She thinks the glass is washed. Her ease depends on it. You find you do not want to be the one to take it from her, and that is a feeling you distrust in yourself.

Her hands shake when she thinks no one is looking, and no one is, but you. Whatever is in that glass, she believes it will ruin her, and a ruined lady and a hanged gentleman are not the same weight on the scale, whatever the law says. You keep catching yourself deciding that for her.

She asked you to wash a glass and say nothing, and she asked it as one woman to another, which is a thing no lady has said to you before. It was either the truth or very well done. The glass is in your pocket. You have not decided which of those it was.

You have begun to learn which of your sentences a drawing room will take and which it will set aside before you have finished them. That is a kind of knowledge too. It is possible to tell the truth so that it is heard, and the truth so that it is not, and you are no longer sure the first is the same as the whole.

Perhaps it need not be said at all. A key in a lock, in front of them, says more than a housekeeper could, and nobody below stairs is asked who put it there. You are not certain whether that is prudence or cowardice, and you are not certain the house will tell the difference when it comes to deciding who stays.

You saw seven people in the wrong places last night, and only one of them killed a man. The others were in the wrong places for reasons of their own: a bed that was not theirs, a letter, a bottle, a debt. Say all of it and the house breaks open and the right name may fall out with the rest. Keep back what does not bear on the study door and you are choosing, for your betters, which of their lies deserve to live. You do not know which of those a servant is permitted to do. You suspect neither.

description.text: The main stair arrives here under a tall window of leaded glass, its half-landing a dozen steps below where the turn makes a place to stop and be seen stopping. A carved newel post stands at the top like a sentry, and the balustrade runs on into the gallery, its rail polished by a century of hands and by yours with a cloth each morning. A brass oil lamp burns on a bracket by day as by night, since the snow light comes grey and gives nothing. The air smells of lamp oil, cold plaster and the wet wool of people who have been outside.

exits.text: You descend with one hand on the rail, the hall's draught rising to meet you at each step.

description.text: A long landing panelled in dark oak, a Turkey runner down its centre and seven bedroom doors along the inner wall, each with a brass number plate and a china finger-plate. Three windows on the outer wall look over the stable yard and the drive, and at night the gallery is lit only by wax candles in brass sconces between the doors. A glass case of stuffed waxwings stands between the second and third windows. It smells of beeswax polish, candle smoke and the damp that comes in at the window frames.

description.text: Past a plaster arch the gallery narrows to a short passage ending at the study door, where the runner stops a yard short and leaves bare boards. A tall mahogany linen press stands against the inner wall, and the gap behind it is the servants' way to the back stairs, a baize-covered door that nobody above stairs is supposed to know about. A leather fire bucket hangs on a hook by the arch. The end window is small and the eaves run close above it, so the sound here is always the roof: snow settling, or water.

description.text: A whitewashed well behind the green baize door, no wider than a man's shoulders, where the servants' passage gives onto the back stairs. A deal shelf at elbow height holds the candle box, and the plaster above it is grey with forty years of tallow smoke from one man's candle. It smells of mutton fat and cold stone, and the only light is what leaks under the baize from the passage. The bell wires run up the corner in their tin casing and tick when anyone upstairs so much as touches a pull.

exits.text: The first tread sounds under your foot, and you take the rope rail in the dark, climbing by touch.

exits.label: into the servants' hall

description.text: Two straight flights of bare deal and a dog-leg turn between them, boxed in by plaster walls close enough to touch with both elbows. A rope rail runs up the inner wall on iron eyes, black and glassy where one hand has gripped it for forty years. There is no window on the flights; the only light is whatever is carried, and the stair gives back every footfall to the gallery above and the passage below. At the top a plain jib door, papered on its far side to match the gallery, lets out at the far end of the first floor.

description.text: A long room panelled in dark oak, with the mahogany table laid for twelve and the master's carver at its head beneath his own portrait. Two tall north windows give a flat grey light that never warms the cloth, and the marble chimneypiece draws badly, so the room smells of coal smoke, beeswax and old gravy. A sideboard runs the length of the inner wall under a row of covered dishes, and the floor creaks at the master's end where the boards have dried over the cellar.

exits.text: You put your shoulder to the service door and it swings on its silent hinge, the table's voices dropping to a murmur behind you.

exits.label: back into the front hall

description.text: A narrow slip of a room behind the service door, shelved to the ceiling with the second-best china and the glass cloths folded in the housekeeper's own way. A lead sink under a small barred window, a scrubbed deal dresser with a locked drawer, and a plate-warmer that ticks as it cools. It smells of soda, damp cloth and the sherry nobody admits to drinking, and from here you can hear every word at the table through the service door.

description.text: A low room off the servants' passage, half office and half bedchamber: a deal desk under the one barred window, a narrow iron bed against the far wall, and a key board of brass hooks beside the door where every lock in the house hangs in rows. The window looks at ground level onto the snow of the kitchen yard, so the light comes in grey and comes in low. The small iron stove in the corner takes the chill off and no more. It smells of blacklead, lavender from the linen cupboard, and the damp that lives in the wall behind the bed.

description.text: A long low room under the front of the house, whitewashed to shoulder height and stone-flagged, with a deal table down its length and benches either side. One high area window lets in a slab of grey snow-light that reaches the table and no farther; the rest is the red of the hearth and tallow. It smells of boiled linen, coal smoke, and the dripping kept in the dresser crock. The house's voices come down to it through the floor as footfalls, never as words.

description.text: A long room of rose-and-fawn paper and horsehair, with a white marble chimneypiece at the centre of the inner wall and two tall windows onto the snowed lawn that let in nothing but grey. A sofa table stands before the fire, a settee and three chairs about it, the Brussels carpet worn to the weave where guests have stood with their backs to the heat. The air is coal smoke and beeswax and damp wool drying. The moderator lamp on the table and the fire are the only warmth of colour in the room; everything else is winter light.

A mahogany coat stand with brass hooks and a stick-well stands against the panelling, a single hall chair beside it, a dinner gong on its frame by the stair. It smells of wet stone, boot-blacking and the snow coming off the step outside. The front door is oak, two bolts and a chain, and the gravel sweep lies beyond it.

The air holds cold ash, stale cigar and lamp oil, and the panelling ticks as the house cools. Grey snow light lies flat across everything and reaches nowhere.

description.text: A brick egg sunk into the bank behind the stable yard, entered through a short tunnel with a door at either end so that the cold does not get out. The ice is stacked in sawn blocks under straw at the far end, and the drain at the centre of the floor ticks as the melt finds it. The air is close and smells of wet brick, straw and the river the ice was cut from. What light there is comes down the tunnel in a grey wedge and goes no further than the slab.

description.text: A long room of oak shelving and dark green paper, the books behind brass-latticed doors nobody has unlocked in years, the carpet worn to its threads in a lane from door to window. The solicitor has taken the great table under the two north windows for his drafting, and the grey snow light lies flat across it all day. The fire here is kept small, as the master liked it, and the room smells of leather bindings, coal smoke and cold ink. The snow stands against the lower panes and everything is heard twice: the clock, the fire, the drip beyond the glass.

description.text: The kitchen yard lies under two days of snow, trodden to a single grey channel between the servants' door and the ice house mound. The pump is frozen to its handle and the coal store door has drifted shut. Wind comes over the stable roof and lifts the loose snow into the face, so that the house behind seems to retreat into white. Somebody has been out here since the last fall: there is a second line of prints, half filled, that does not go to the ice house at all.

description.text: Carved oak, an acorn finial worn smooth on the stair side where people rest a hand before going down. Someone has leaned here long enough lately to leave a smear of face powder on the acorn.

The balustrade runs from the newel along the whole gallery, and from this corner a man standing at it can see the hall below and every door behind him. You polish it each morning; this morning there is a watch-chain scratch in the wax.
Tall leaded glass a dozen steps down, the only window on the stair, with the roof's edge just above it. Snow sits against the outer panes in a wedge that has grown for two days.
Brass rods holding the Turkey carpet to each tread. The third from the top is loose in its eye and rings when trodden; the household knows to step over it, and guests do not.
A banjo barometer in walnut, the needle stuck at Change. The glass over the dial is dulled in one spot where the master tapped it every morning on his way down.
A brass oil lamp with a white glass shade, kept burning because the stair would be black without it. You filled it yourself at six; the level is lower than one day's burning should leave it.
Number four, the best guest room, nearest the stair. The china finger-plate is clean except for a thumb's smear of blacking low on the panel, at the height of a boot held in one hand.
Number six, Mr Yardley's since he was a boy at school. The key is on the inside; the keyhole shows a sliver of light when his lamp is lit, and the bottom rail is scuffed from being kicked shut.
Number two, Mrs Ormsby's, across from the second window. The door does not sit true and must be pulled hard to latch, so it cannot be closed quietly by anyone who does not know it.
Three sashes over the stable yard and the sweep of the drive, grey with snow light by day. From the middle one you can see the yard door and the path to the ice house, and whoever crosses them.

Brass wall sconces between the doors, each with a white wax candle. Above stairs burns wax; below stairs burns tallow, and the two leave different stubs and different smells. The sconce by number four has a drip of something yellower on its tray.
Red and ochre, worn to the weave outside the Major's and the nephew's doors and hardly at all outside the others. Damp footmarks dry out of it slowly in this cold, and you have learned to read them.
A glass case of stuffed waxwings on a branch, dusty inside, a card in the master's father's hand: Shot in the great snow, 1838. One bird has lost its glass eye and looks at the gallery with a hole.

Heavy oak, panelled, with a brass escutcheon over the mortice lock. The keyhole is wide enough to take a lamp's light through, and the escutcheon is rubbed bright at the bottom edge where a cheek has pressed against it more than once.

A yard of unpolished board between the end of the runner and the study door, dark with age. Low down, where a kneeling person's knee and skirt would rest, the dust is disturbed in two places, not one.

A tall mahogany press of sheets and pillow-slips, lavender between the folds. Behind it, a baize-covered door lets onto the servants' passage to the back stairs; the press stands an inch off the wall, enough for a candle's glow to show along its edge.

A leather bucket on a hook, filled with sand and painted with the house's crest in flaking red. It has hung here since the kitchen chimney went up in the master's father's time, and nobody has lifted it since.
A small square sash under the eaves, the sill wet from the frame leaking. From it you hear the roof before you see anything: snow settling with a sigh, or the drip when it begins to go.

A small brass bell on a sprung wire beside the study door, rung from the desk inside for the valet alone. The wire has been oiled so often that it does not creak; Fairbrother came whenever it moved, and now it does not move.

A deal box with a sliding lid, greasy at the thumb-place, holding the yellow tallow dips the servants draw by. The dips lie in rows of six; the box is squared to the shelf edge so exactly that the dust line shows if it has been moved a quarter-inch.

A plank of deal on two brackets, set at the height of a tall man's elbow, not a housekeeper's. A pale rectangle in the grease marks where the box sits, and a smaller ring beside it where a candlestick is set down each night.

Green baize over deal on a spring, to swallow the sound of the servants' side. The spring is strong enough to shut it on a skirt, and the baize is worn to the cloth at the one place a shoulder goes through with hands full.
A tongue of grey soot on the whitewash above the shelf, laid down over forty years by a candle lifted and set in the same place. It is the height of Fairbrother's hand at rest, and no one else's.

Four wires in a tin casing up the corner, each one lettered in old ink: Study, Master's Room, Blue Room, Gallery. The Study wire is bright where the others are dull, as if it has been pulled more than any of them, or lately.
An iron hook in the wall at the foot of the first tread where the housemaid hangs her ash pail between rounds. The whitewash below it is streaked grey from a pail set down wet and emptied in haste.
Nine treads of bare deal, the fourth and seventh scooped hollow in the middle and silent, the rest giving a dry crack underfoot. Someone who climbs here nightly would know which to step on.

Tarred rope on iron eyes, black and smooth as horn along the inner wall. There is a bright ravelled place near the turn where a ring or a button has caught the fibres, recently enough that the loose ends are still pale.

A square of boards where the flights meet, the corner of the plaster rubbed through to the brown beneath by shoulders turning in the dark. A spot of yellow grease has dried on the top board here, where a dip was set down and taken up again.

A long smear of soot along the upper flight's wall at a steady height, where a candle has been carried close to the plaster on every climb. It breaks off two treads from the top, where the carrier has learned to lift it clear of the jib door.

A plain deal door on the stair side, papered and skirted on the gallery side so that from the first floor it is only a seam in the wall. The thumb-latch is worn silver, and the door shuts with a sound no louder than a book closing.

The second tread from the top rocks on its riser and knocks once when weight comes off it. A wedge of folded paper has been pushed under one end to quiet it, yellowed, and pushed in from the stair side.
The carver at the head of the table, its arms worn pale where he gripped them to rise. A fold of the cloth beside it is kept clear of plate, as though a place were still laid for a hand to rest on.
Damask, double-laid, with the house crest woven at the master's end. A faint ring near the head, where something warm was set down without a mat, has not come out in two launderings.
Mahogany, long enough to stand four at once with their backs to the table. From here you can see every face at dinner in the mirror behind the covers, and nobody at the table thinks to look at you.
The big Worcester soup tureen with the chipped lid, heavy enough to need two hands. Held out an instant too long, it hides whatever the mouth of the one holding it is doing.
Horn-handled knife and fork in a baize-lined case on the sideboard. The master kept them sharp himself; the blade has a hair's turn at the point where he was careless once.
The master at forty, hand on a dog that died before you came. The eyes are painted to follow the room, and from the sideboard they rest on his own empty chair.
A wide iron basket under the marble chimneypiece, with a fender that is kicked more than polished. The coal scuttle beside it is marked with the hour it was last filled, in Lavinia's chalk.
Two tall sashes with the shutters folded back into the panelling. A line of gravel drive is just visible past the cedar, so whoever sits at the master's right sees the carriage before anyone else.
The locked drawer of the deal dresser, the one key on your ring that has no label. It smells of wax and sherry when it opens, and the runners stick an inch from closed unless lifted just so.
A small cut glass with a brown ring dried in the bowl and a smear on the rim the width of a lip. Unwashed, it still keeps an hour nobody has given you.
Green baize on the dining-room side, bare deal on this. It is hung to swing silently, and a servant standing with her ear a hand's breadth from it is invisible to the table.
A shallow lead trough under the barred window, with a brass tap that must be held open. Glasses are washed here last, and whoever washes them is the last to see what was in them.
A japanned tin cabinet on legs with a spirit lamp beneath, ticking as it cools. The lamp was lit for dinner the night the master died and nobody remembered to put it out.
Linen cloths folded in thirds on the shelf, each marked in the corner with a stitched letter. One, with the previous housekeeper's initial, has been turned so the mark faces the wall.
The papier-mâché tea tray with the mother-of-pearl rose, the one Lavinia carries up and the one that comes back with a cup you did not ring for.

Brass hooks in six rows, each labelled in the old housekeeper's hand: cellar, plate, linen, study, the guest rooms by name. The study hook is polished brighter than the rest, and there is one hook at the end with no label and no key.
A long ruled ledger of candles, coals, soap and wages, kept to the farthing. The last page in the old housekeeper's hand stops mid-week, and the tallow column for that week was never totted.

A wooden travelling box with iron corners and your initials painted on the lid, standing at the foot of the bed where it was set down the day you came. The hasp is good, but the lock is the kind any gentleman's penknife could lift.
A plain desk scrubbed white, with a pen tray, a blotter and a shallow well for the ink. Someone before you has scored a tally in the near edge, five strokes and a bar, and not gone on with it.
A narrow bedstead with a horsehair mattress and two grey blankets folded to the hospital corner. The wall behind it is stained with damp in the shape of a county nobody can name.
Four iron bars and a sill at the level of the yard, so you see boots before you see faces. The snow outside is trodden to the coal-hole and no further.
A small iron stove with a mica door and a kettle that lives on top of it. The ash drawer below has been emptied so often the catch is worn to a nub.
A black straw bonnet still on its peg behind the door, the ribbons faded brown. Nobody told you whether Mrs. Dacre died or left, and nobody has asked for it.
Twelve feet of deal scrubbed pale, with a dark ring at the cook's end where the teapot has stood for thirty years. The near corner is worn to a shine by wrists held against it.

A black-painted board lettered in white: no followers, no singing, no servant to be above stairs after the family is up without a bell. Beneath the last rule someone has pencilled a small, neat date and rubbed most of it out.
Fourteen brass bells on coiled springs, each with a painted room name beneath. The study bell's spring is stretched longer than the rest, and its clapper hangs still.
An open coal fire behind an iron fender, the hob kept for the staff kettle. The ash in the pan here is grey and fine; study ash, with its paper, would be flecked black.

A plain pine dresser of blue-rimmed plates and a brown dripping crock. The second hook from the end holds a servant's cup with a chipped foot, turned to the wall as cups are when their owner has left under a cloud.
The only chair with arms, at the head of the table, its cushion flattened to the shape of one woman. Nobody sits in it, even when she is upstairs.
A high sash set into the area wall, iron-barred on the outside, snow banked against the lower panes. From the bench you can see only boots pass, never faces.
A thin ruled book kept on the dresser shelf, names down the side and quarter-days across. Lavinia Netherby's line shows two quarters paid and a third left blank.
A mahogany sofa table drawn before the fire, its leather top ringed by other winters' glasses. Whatever is laid on it is seen by everyone sitting round; that is what it is for.
White marble, a Carrington crest cut into the frieze, a fire that someone keeps built high. Stand at the settee and the heat reaches your face; stand at the door and it does not.
Two mahogany leaves with brass finger-plates, polished where the master's hand went for twenty years and dull where a servant's would. A man standing beside them is in the room and out of it at once.
A black marble clock under a glass dome, stopped at twenty past eleven. It has not been wound since the night, and nobody has offered to.
A brass oil lamp with a green shade, its chimney smoked on one side. Turned up, it throws the faces round the table into relief and leaves the corners.
Miss Davenport's basket, lid open, a half-finished slipper in Berlin wool. The needle is threaded with a colour she has not used in the pattern.

A cushioned seat under the east window, the velvet faded in a long oval where the master sat to watch the drive. From it the lawn is a sheet of grey with the drive a darker line, dripping now at the edges.
A japanned scuttle with a brass handle, filled to the lip. Somebody has made up this fire more often than the maid's rounds account for.
Mahogany, six brass hooks, a stick-well below. A gentleman's coat hung here hangs with its pockets at a woman's eye level.
Oak, two bolts and a chain, the lower bolt stiff with snow-swell. Through the fanlight the sweep is visible, and whether anything has turned on the gravel.
A worn stone step under the porch, swept twice a day and drifted over between. Boots that come in by it leave their water on the flags in a line any servant can read.
A single carved hall chair, hard oak with the crest on its back, never meant for comfort. It is where one waits for a carriage, or to be told whether one may go.
A brass gong on a turned frame, the beater hung beside it. Fairbrother struck it at seven every night for forty years; the dent is dead centre.
An oil lantern on a chain, its glass fogged with cold. It makes a small warm circle on the flags and leaves the door in grey.
A silver salver on the side table with the week's cards still on it, the topmost Mrs Gresham's, its corner turned down in the old way to say she called in person.
A heavy brass rim lock on the room side of the door, its keyhole a clean black slot a finger wide. With a key standing in it from this side, nothing at all can be seen through from the gallery.

A brass colza lamp with a green glass shade on the writing table, set at the master's left hand so its light fell straight across the room to the door. The reservoir is near dry; it burned a long while after anyone needed it.
A single grey spot of hardened tallow on the hearthrug, a yard inside the door. This is a wax-candle room; tallow lives on the back stairs.
A broad oak table with a tooled leather top and a blotter whose pink sheet has been turned recently. Held to the window, the blotter gives back a few words in reverse, a date and half a signature.
Three cut-glass decanters locked in an oak frame, the little key gone from its hook. Two decanters are full; the third stands a finger lower than the others, its stopper set back slightly crooked.
A worn crimson pull beside the chimneypiece, its tassel grey from forty years of one hand. It rings the master's bell in the servants' hall and nowhere else.
A framed survey of the park and farms, hung where the master could see it from his chair. The home farm and two fields have been shaded in pencil, and a figure written and rubbed out in the margin.
A low brass fender before the cold fireplace, the rail dented on the left side where something heavy came down against it. The dent has been there long enough to tarnish.

The master, under the sheet from his own bed, laid straight on the slate with his hands folded as Fairbrother would have wanted. The nails of the right hand are broken short and there is a bruise on the inside of the wrist the colour of a plum, older than the night he died.

A slate shelf on two brick piers where the cook lays game and the fishmonger's basket in summer. Someone has scrubbed it before the master was put on it, and the wet has frozen to a grey bloom along the edge.

A black gladstone open on the straw, instruments rolled in chamois, a case of glass tubes with cork stoppers. Tucked in the lid is a folded letter in the master's hand, the seal broken some weeks ago by the look of the wax.

A flat morocco case propped on an ice block to keep the ink off the wet, a steel pen laid across a half-written sheet. Ellingham has written the date and the word 'deposition' and then nothing, the pen waiting on what you say.

River ice sawn into blocks the size of a hat box and bedded in straw to the curve of the dome. The top course has been disturbed; the straw is pushed back and one block is gone, the hollow where it sat already glazing over.

An iron grating over the centre of the floor, where the melt goes down to the river. Something has been poured through it recently: the brick around the grate is clean where the rest is furred with green.

Dates in chalk on the brick beside the tunnel door, one for every filling since the ice house was dug, the earliest in a hand that is not Fairbrother's but is very like it. The last date is this January; under it someone has drawn a small cross and rubbed it out again.

Oak sheathed in zinc, with a sliding bolt on the yard side only. The snow has drifted against it to the latch, and there is one set of prints in the drift besides your own, coming from the house and not going back.

A great mahogany table with a green leather top, the leather worn pale at the one place a man sits to write. The solicitor's blotting pad lies squared to the edge; held to the window, its reverse shows every signature he has taken in the house, backwards.
A heavy cut-glass inkstand with two wells and a pen tray, the black well full, the red well dried to a crust. Whatever is written here is written in the master's ink.
A japanned tin box lettered CARRINGTON in faded gilt, with a lock the solicitor keeps the key to on his watch chain. Papers put into it leave the house's keeping and enter the law's.
A brass wax jack with a coil of red sealing wax and a spirit flame. The seal beside it is the master's; the solicitor has turned it face down on the leather.
A set of folding mahogany steps left at the far bookcase, their top tread dusty but for two clean marks the width of a pair of shoes.
A winged chair by the fire, the horsehair gone flat on the left arm where he rested a glass. Nobody has sat in it since Tuesday; the guests take the sofa and leave it empty, as if he might come in.

A run of shelf beside the fire where the oak is blackened in a crescent and the books behind the lattice have cockled spines. A lamp went over there once; the old housekeeper's rule about open flames in this room dates from it.
A man's boot, by the size, going out toward the stable wall and coming back, filled to half their depth. The snow stopped at four this morning; they were made before that.
Frozen solid, the handle furred with ice. Nobody has drawn water here since the storm began; the kitchen has been melting snow.

Thirty-one keys on an iron ring, every door in the house but one. The study key is not among them; he kept it on his own watch-chain and told you, not unkindly, that you should have it when he had finished with it. The ring is heavy at your waist and you have learned to walk so it does not sound.

A cut-glass tumbler, wrapped in a tea-cloth and lying in the bottom of your apron pocket, unwashed. There is a dried ring in the bottom of it and something else, a smell under the brandy, that you cannot put a name to and are not certain you want to. A lady asked you to rinse it and say nothing. You have done neither, yet.

Gold gone thin, on a bit of black ribbon inside your collar; housekeepers do not wear rings on the hand. It is the whole of what you brought from the smaller house, that and a character written by a mistress who was sorry to lose you and said so in two lines.

A finger's length of cheap yellow tallow, snuffed hard, standing in the study's mantel candlestick among the white wax that is all the master ever burned. It is the servants' candle; the box it came from is on a shelf at the foot of the back stair.
A gold hunter, open on the white cloth with its chain laid across the master's empty place. Its hands say ten past eight. It is the only clock in the house the Major has not let anyone else wind.
Your own apron: keys on their ring, a thimble, black thread, and in the left pocket under the keys the tallow stub from the study hearth.
A jet hairpin, black against the bare boards, an inch below the study keyhole.
Lavinia's housemaid's pail, empty, the rim still wet. Beside it the fresh scuttle for a dead man's fire.
Your small black book of the night's rounds: every door tried, every hour, every name on every landing. The only record in the house of where everyone was.
The tallow box from the butler's pantry, brought up and set on the sofa table. Twelve slots. Eleven candles, white and unburnt.
A single sheet in a soldier's upright hand, headed 'An Account of the Night'. It puts Lucius Carrington in his bed from half past ten.
A tortoiseshell hairpin in a twist of paper, labelled in the solicitor's hand: 'Found at the study keyhole. C.E.'
A corner torn from a letter, folded twice, the pencil pressed through the paper so the words can be read from the back.
Through the ajar door: the grate still holds its ash from the night the master died, grey and unraked, waiting for the pails.
A cup poured for you and left on the dresser, gone lukewarm, the only thing in the room nobody is looking at.
Heavy military cloth on the coat stand, sagging to one side. The right pocket holds something wrapped in a napkin, the size and weight of a sherry glass.
Ellingham's hand, still wet: the quarrel at eleven by the Major's watch, the lady's candle on the back stair. There is nothing on it about a key.
A cup of tea on the housekeeper's table, strong, the way the kitchen has learnt you take it. The steam stands straight up in the cold.
Your rounds book, open at the murder night: the quarrel at half past ten, one flame on the back stairs at eleven, and a line left for the hour of the last candle.
A kitchen sieve, mesh gone grey. It shakes in Lavinia's hands, and a fine ash falls through it onto the bare boards.
Set down on the stair-rods where the maids dropped it when the lawyer called them down. Thaw water has got into it and drips wet coal onto the carpet.
Your own ewer, full of water drawn before the Major barred the stair. The water is very cold.
Brewed on your own spirit lamp behind the door; the only tea in the house this morning not poured by a maid.

A papered door at the back of your room, opening on a black passage that comes out behind the linen press on the study end. Fairbrother lit the Major along it two nights since. He has not mentioned it.
A long iron key with a worn brass bow, hung on the Major's waistcoat chain beside his watch. It is the only key to the study, and it has been in his pocket since the night the door was found locked.
An inch of kitchen tallow, burnt down and gone out, lying on the bare boards a yard from the study door. The sconces here take wax. Nobody who belongs on this floor carries tallow.

A half sheet in Mr Yardley's hand, the ink barely dry. It says you are honest in your accounts and that a woman who put her hand in a gentleman's pocket cannot be kept. It is signed. It will get you nothing.

C01.name: Lucius Carrington

description.text: He has your rounds book under his hand like a duty roster, and when you come in he does not look up; he says the hour he wants and waits for you to write it, as a man does with a sergeant who will.
He stands between you and the main stair without seeming to, and his eyes go to your apron pockets before they go to your face; he has begun to count what you carry.
The colour has gone out of his face in a single stripe under each eye, and his hands, which have given every order in this house for two days, hang at his sides with nothing to do.
The nephew has his arms; the key stands in the lock behind him; and he is looking not at the key but at his own right hand, as if it had acted without leave.
He sits in the master's chair with the master's carving knife and the master's key already across the cloth to you; he fills the chair as if he had been measuring it for thirty years.

Sixty-odd, upright as a post, a clipped white moustache and a weathered red face; the ribbon of his decoration is the one bright thing on his black, and his watch chain lies straight across a waistcoat that sits heavier on one side.

here.text: The Major has his watch open in his palm and is looking past you for whoever he means to send next.
The Major stands with his back to the fire and his hands clasped behind him, and does not turn his head when you come in.
The Major stands at parade rest with the ribbon at his breast and one thumb hooked in his waistcoat pocket.

says.text: 'Fell from the inside lock when the door went. The whole gallery heard it land. You'll put that in the hours exactly so.' He pats the waistcoat pocket once and goes back to the roster.
'The key is in a gentleman's keeping and will go to the magistrate in a gentleman's hand. A housekeeper has no questions about it.' He does not raise his voice. 'Below, now.'
'It was on his chain.' He says it to the fire, not to the room. 'He never took it off. Not in thirty years.'
'Inside lock, door bolted from within, key on the carpet by the jamb. That's a locked room, and that's the end of the matter.' He looks at the clock, not at you.
'Quarrelled with his uncle at eleven, was heard at it, and ran for the stables at the first word of a cart. I've seen men bolt under fire. It tells you all you need.' He nods you toward the door.
'The young gentleman has a lawyer now, and a housekeeper, it seems.' He weighs you with a look. 'I hope he pays better than his uncle did.'
'Young Yardley owes money in town and his uncle knew it. Mr Ellingham will have the sum. The rest is for the magistrate at thaw.' He makes it sound like a march already ordered.

'He was dying. Ashcombe will tell you so. He meant to write to the regiment before Christmas, and he called me up to say it to my face, like a gentleman.' He stops there, and nobody asks him to go on.
'Thirty years he never said a word of it. Not at mess, not at table, not in his cups.' His voice stays level. 'He waited till he was dying to be honest. I call that cowardice too.'

'Best officer I served under and the only man in England who never asked me for anything.' A pause a beat too long. 'Fairbrother will have his boots done. See the fires are kept up on the gallery; he hated a cold house.'

'Quarrel at eleven, lights out by half past, nothing on the back stairs after. You read it in that order and you stop when I say stop.' He taps the page once. 'Clean account. The magistrate likes a clean account.'
'Your hours are the household's. They go to me, not to a lawyer, and not into a drawer with whatever else you keep there.' He holds his hand out for the book and waits.

'A housekeeper's rounds are the one honest clock in a house like this. Mind you keep them so.' He glances at his watch, then at you. 'Half past ten? You were new that night. You'll have misheard the chime.'
'Eleven by my watch, and I set it against the hall clock Sunday. Miss Davenport heard it; you heard it. That's two, and two is sufficient.' He closes the case.
'Eleven. Miss Davenport's word, my watch, and the hall clock that struck through the study door. I don't want to hear a housekeeper's half past ten at table again.'
He puts his hand over it as if it were a wound. 'He was there. He saw what it was for.' Nothing more.
'Thirty years on the ribbon. He stood beside me the day it was pinned.' He brushes it with two fingers. 'Don't have the maid polish it. I do that myself.'
'The valet answers to me while the house is without a master. Not to a housekeeper of a fortnight's standing. You'll leave him be.' He says it quietly, which is worse.
'Forty years. He'd have gone to his grave with it if nobody asked.' He looks at the old man by the door for the first time all day. 'I counted on that. God forgive me, I counted on it.'
'Steadiest man in the house. Forty years and never a question he wasn't asked. You'd want him in a line.' He frowns at the back stair. 'Leave him his habits. He has few enough left.'

'A glass in a housekeeper's drawer is evidence or it is blackmail, and I've not decided which. You'll decide it for me in the drawing room at three.' He snaps his watch shut. 'A lady at ten and the quarrel after. That's all the room needs.'
'Miss Gresham tells me you keep a lady's glass unwashed in a drawer. A servant who holds things over a guest's head is a servant with a short character.' He lets that stand.
'A lady's sherry at ten is a lady's business and nobody's else. Least of all the housekeeper's.' He turns to the window. 'Wash it and have done.'

'Ashcombe puts the death between eleven and one and wanted brandy after saying it. A regimental surgeon would have given me the half-hour before he reached for the bottle. Two hours is no use to a magistrate.'
'Miss Gresham has a good eye for what goes into a servant's apron. She has reported it to me. I'd mind that, if I were you, next time you're near the study.'
'Miss Gresham means to be mistress of this house within the year and is weighing the staff already. Serve her as you'd serve the mistress. It saves changing habits later.'
'The ward keeps time like a quartermaster's wife. Eleven, she says, voices through the study door. A girl who has just lost her guardian does not invent the hour, and I'll hold the table on it.'
'Mrs Ormsby was at the piano until the shouting stopped her hands. She'll sign her statement without argument; widows know what a house sounds like with a dead man in it. Take hers first.'
'The maid laid the study fire at six and swears to white wax in the sticks. Nervous girl. Nervous girls miscount. Keep her below and off the gallery; I'll not have her fainting on the carpet.'
'Ellingham is paid by the estate. The estate is the nephew. You carried your hours to him and not to me, and I note it.'
'Ellingham draws the papers up. He does not decide what goes in them. A clerk with a better coat and a worse constitution.'
'Quarles waded up at dawn to report the road. The one man on this estate who came and told me a thing without being sent for. Noon, he says, and I'll take his word over the doctor's.'
'One corridor. Bedroom doors along it, the study at the end, a window beyond. Whoever went to that door walked that carpet, and I have posted men on worse ground than a gallery.'
'I sent you below and you came up the valet's stairs. I do not forget a man who leaves his post. Nor a woman.'
'Servants' stairs. They come out at the valet's door by the study end. Fairbrother's route for forty years. Not yours.'
'We dine at eight. A house keeps its hours or it comes to pieces, same as a mess. Lay the master's place and leave the chair empty.'
'Your room. I'll want to see inside it before the magistrate does.'
'Your room, your keys, your book. Keep the door locked. Miss Gresham has been through it already in her head.'
'I do not go below. Not my ground. You carry my orders down and bring the maids' answers up; that is the arrangement and it has served.'
'The account is read there and signed there. Fire built up, chairs in a row, Ellingham at the writing table. I want the house to hear it once, together, before the carriage comes round.'

'The room stands as it was found until I say otherwise. Nobody in, nothing out. I'll send the maids up with pails when I judge it; a magistrate shouldn't be handed a room two days cold and stinking of ash.'
'Ashcombe and I carried him down ourselves. A man is not left at his desk for two days whatever the coroner prefers. It is forty yards from the kitchen door; keep the maids from it.'
'I had the port in the library until half past ten by my watch, then went up. Mrs Ormsby passed the door; ask her. I've no objection to my own hours being checked. They stand.'

'I gave the order for the poker. Three strokes, hinge side, and a thing dropped on the carpet inside before the door went. Window fast, fire dead. I've seen men dead in the field with less to go on and the matter settled by noon.'

'A man with a clear conscience sits through his soup. The boy ran for the stables in a snowstorm and we fetched him back half dead. I had him locked in for his own preservation as much as the house's.'
'Noon for the road, Quarles says. Account read at ten, carriage at half past eleven, pails to the study at nine. Write the hours down; I'll not have the day drift.'
'I keep my door shut and my watch on the table beside the bed. I heard the quarrel through it as any man on the gallery would. Questions about my door come to me, not to the maids.'
'Locked, and Fairbrother on the hall chair outside it. It stays locked until the magistrate. Not punishment. Custody. There is a difference and the boy will learn it.'
'Two inches of oak and it took the poker and three men. Nobody slipped through that. It is off its hinge now; I've had the frame left as it broke so the magistrate can see the work.'
'Frozen fast. I put my own shoulder to it the morning we broke in and it did not give a quarter inch. Nobody came by the window. Strike it off and move on.'
'A table wants a head or it goes to pieces. Somebody carves. Until the estate is settled it will be me, and I'll thank the house not to make a drama of it.'
'Nobody sits in it. Lay the place, leave the chair. The regiment does the same for a fallen colonel.'
'The cloth stays over him. Ashcombe put it there and he was right to. A man's face is not for the maids to carry about the house.'
'I am told things find their way into that drawer. When I ask for it open, I'll expect it open.'
'Your drawer is your business until the magistrate asks for the wages book. Keep it in order. That is all.'
'Clean page. Write it as I give it, hour by my watch, and sign at the foot. A plain record, properly kept, is worth more to a magistrate than seven gentlefolk remembering.'
'You have been writing in that book what I did not dictate. I have seen the pencil going. Bring it up.'
'Bring the book to the drawing room at ten. We shall want it read aloud.'
'When I have the maids questioned, sit them along one side of it. A row is easier to watch than a ring. Any sergeant will tell you.'
'That chair is Fairbrother's post outside the nephew's door. He has sat in a hall forty years for one master; he can sit two nights for another's heir without a cushion.'
'The lock was turned from inside. The door came down, and what was in it fell. That is what a locked room means and I'll not have it argued by people who have never held a position.'

C01.history: Lucius Carrington served thirty years beside the master and wears a decoration for a day under fire the master never once spoke of at table. He went up the back stairs at eleven behind the valet's tallow candle to be told the regiment would hear of that day before Christmas, and came down without the candle, with the master's key in his pocket. Since the door came down he has given the house its orders, and means the household's hours to say what his watch says.

C02.name: Reginald Fairbrother
C02.role: the master's valet of forty years

description.text: He stands a half-step nearer than a valet need stand to a housekeeper, and when you pass the tallow box he has already turned it so the lid faces you, as he would for the master's own hand.
He keeps the candle box under his arm now rather than on its shelf, and he addresses the air a foot to the left of your cap, the way he speaks to tradesmen at the kitchen door.
He has said it, and it shows in his hands: they hang at his sides with nothing to do, no candle, no boots, no box, for the first time in forty years that you have seen.
His head is lower than it was two days ago, and his coat is brushed as carefully as ever, and he has started pairing boots outside doors that nobody will open.
A spare, grey man past sixty in a black coat gone brown at the seams, a stub of candle always in one hand, who has learned to stand so still in a doorway that the family forgot he was there.

here.text: Fairbrother has the candle box under his arm and his eyes on the stair, not on you.
Fairbrother has his candle held low so it lights your way as much as his.
Fairbrother has a pair of the master's boots over one arm, blacked, with nobody to wear them.
Fairbrother stands with a lit tallow candle cupped in one hand and his coat buttoned to the throat.

says.text: 'Two dozen on a Monday, drawn by Fairbrother alone after ten, and the housekeeper has leave to count it whenever she pleases.' He sets the lid back on. 'She will find it as he left it, and she will know what that means without his saying.'

'The box has been Fairbrother's keeping since before the housekeeper was in long skirts.' He does not open it. 'If the count is wanted she may ask the heir for it, since she seems fond of going to him.'

'Servants' tallow, two dozen the week, the box kept on the back stair so the maids need not come up for it.' He turns the stub in his fingers. 'The study burns wax, if that is what the housekeeper is asking.'

hour_he_drew_the_last_candle.label: the hour he drew the last candle

says.text: 'Eleven, by the hall clock, and he lit the Major up and went down and said nothing, as he was told.' He looks at you for once. 'The housekeeper has it now; she had better keep it more carefully than he did.'

A long pause, the candle guttering between you. 'The master gave Fairbrother an order that night, and the order was to say nothing of it.' He does not look away. 'He would ask the housekeeper not to make him choose which of them he serves.'
'The housekeeper asks a great many hours of the household.' He pinches the candle out. 'Fairbrother has been asked once by the Major, and has not been asked by anyone whose business it was.'

'The last candle was drawn after ten, as it always is.' He waits, and offers nothing more. 'If the housekeeper means some other question she had better ask it plainly, and then she will have asked it.'

'He was a hard man to dress and an easy man to serve, and he knew the difference better than most.' He is quiet a moment. 'He had been coughing blood into his handkerchiefs since Michaelmas, and told Fairbrother to burn them, and Fairbrother did.'

'Shaved at seven, dressed by the half-hour, a cold bath winter and summer, and no one in the study after ten but by his ringing.' He straightens the candle in its stick. 'That is the master, and that is all the housekeeper needs of him.'

'Major Carrington was in this house every Christmas for thirty years, and Fairbrother blacked his boots every one of them.' His mouth works. 'He would thank the housekeeper not to ask him whether he is sorry.'

'The master's oldest friend, and the master sent for him that night by name.' He lowers his voice below the stair. 'Whatever the housekeeper thinks she saw, Fairbrother would ask her to remember who it was that did the sending.'

'The Major has given orders in this house before, when the master was from home, and the house has obeyed them.' He looks past you to the gallery. 'Fairbrother does not see that anything is different now.'

'Mr. Yardley crossed the yard at twenty to eleven; Fairbrother saw him from the boot room window and said nothing, because nobody asked.' He shifts on the hall chair. 'He has sat outside that boy's door since he had the measles, and he does not care for the key.'
'Fairbrother sits where he is put, and the Major put him here.' He does not rise. 'The young gentleman has had his supper, and has thrown it at the wall, and the wall will be seen to in the morning.'

'He was dying, and he knew it, and the doctor knew it, and Fairbrother knew it from the handkerchiefs.' He says it low and to the candle. 'He would be obliged if the housekeeper let him say that to the family himself, when it is wanted, and not before.'

'The master's health was the master's business and the doctor's.' He turns to go. 'The housekeeper has been three weeks in the house; she will forgive him if he does not take her into it in the fourth.'
'He ate less this winter and rang for the fire more.' A pause. 'Fairbrother had the chemist's bottles to dust, and dusted them, and that is as far as his place went.'

'Mrs. Pell kept this house twenty years and never once went up the back stair after dark; the housekeeper has been up it twice in a night.' He almost nods. 'Fairbrother told the master a woman from outside would not do, and he will say now that he was wrong, and he does not say it often.'

'The master engaged the housekeeper without consulting his valet, which was his right.' He speaks to the candle flame. 'Fairbrother had a name to put forward, and was not asked for it, and has said all he means to on the matter.'

'The Major has had the blue room eleven Christmases and takes his own boots off outside the door, which a gentleman does not. His own man never comes with him.' He pauses. 'He knows this house as well as the family, and better than some.'
'The Major is a guest of the house. Fairbrother treats him as one and would counsel the housekeeper to do the same, while she is housekeeper.'
'Major Carrington has had the blue room eleven Christmases. He rings for shaving water at seven and does not ring again. Fairbrother is asked nothing further and says nothing further.'

'Fairbrother has cleaned Mr. Nathaniel's boots since he was in short coats. He has never once said thank you and never once needed telling where a thing was kept. He is not a running sort of young gentleman, whatever the yard saw on Thursday.'

'Dr. Ashcombe dines twice a quarter and sat up three nights in March when the master's chest was bad. He drinks the master's port as though he expects to be paid in it. Fairbrother decants it all the same.'

'Miss Gresham rings for hot water at seven and again at the half hour, and is dressed before either can arrive. Fairbrother does not know what a young lady does with a half hour she has already used. He only carries the cans.'

'Miss Evangeline has the run of the library and the old dog and the master's temper when she wanted it. She was the one person under this roof he did not raise his voice to.' He straightens a glove on the tray. 'Fairbrother does not say that lightly.'
'Mrs. Ormsby takes the yellow room for her knees, it being nearest the stairs. Her knees managed the gallery quick enough when the poker was called for. She was at the door before the doctor.'

'Netherby does the first-floor grates and does them properly, and has been crying into the ash since Thursday. She was on the back stairs later than a housemaid should be.' He stops there. 'Fairbrother does not ask maids why they cry. That is the housekeeper's province now, and he would sooner it were asked kindly.'
'Netherby does the first-floor grates and does them properly, and has been crying into the ash since Thursday. Fairbrother does not ask maids why they cry. That is the housekeeper's province now.'

'Mr. Ellingham came up on the Tuesday with a bag he has not let out of his sight and sleeps with his boots by the bed as if he means to leave in them. He has twice asked Fairbrother whether the master's desk locks.' A slow breath. 'It does.'

'Quarles has kept the lodge thirty years and has never once come up to the house without being sent for. This morning he walked four feet of snow to the kitchen door without being sent for. Fairbrother gave him tea and did not ask.'

'Eleven doors and the master's at the end of it. Fairbrother has walked that gallery with a candle more nights than the housekeeper has been alive. The boards speak outside the Major's door and go quiet outside the widow's; one learns where to put one's feet.'

'The back stairs are for the household and the coals, and for such guests as do not care to be met on the front. The lamp there is not lit after ten. Anyone wanting to go up after ten takes a candle from the shelf, and the shelf has tallow, not wax.'

'Fairbrother has drawn out the master's chair at the head of that table every evening for twenty years. On Thursday no one had told him not to, and he drew it out, and it sat there empty through five courses with the Major talking across it.'

'Mrs. Pell had that room twenty-two years. Her chair is still turned to the fire the way she liked it, and the key of the store cupboard still hangs on the second hook, not the first.' He does not look at you. 'Fairbrother would be obliged if both were left so.'
'The hall takes its tone from the top of the table. It has been very quiet at the top of the table these two days, and the boy has stopped whistling. Fairbrother is aware of it.'

'The drawing-room fire is kept up for the ladies. The Major has taken the chair nearest it, which was the master's chair, and has not been told so. Fairbrother did not consider it his place to tell him.'

'Fairbrother laid the study fire and two white wax candles at six every evening for forty years. White wax from the chandler at Lichfield. The master would not have tallow in that room; the smell got into the books.'

'Dr. Ashcombe asked whether the ice house would take a man. Fairbrother told him it would take a side of beef, and the doctor took that for his answer. The path to it has not been cleared, and Fairbrother has not been asked to clear it.'

'The library shares a chimney with the study. On a still night a person in the one can hear a chair pushed back in the other.' He considers the window. 'Thursday was not a still night. Miss Evangeline was in there until the candles went, as she always is.'

'The Major called for the poker before anyone had tried the handle twice. Fairbrother heard the key go down on the carpet inside before the wood gave. He has been asked since whether he is sure of that. He has dropped enough keys on enough carpets to know the sound.'

'Fairbrother served the soup and heard the word magistrate before the fish. Mr. Nathaniel went out by the service door, which he has not used since he was a boy stealing jam. Fairbrother had him by the collar in the yard, and was told to sit at his door, and sat.'

'The Major sent Netherby up with a scuttle to a dead man's grate. Fairbrother went up behind her and stood in the study doorway until she had finished, so that nothing went into her pail that was not ash. He then came down to be sent for.'

'The blue-room door drops on its hinges in wet weather and must be lifted to shut quietly, or it bangs. It did not bang on Thursday night. The Major has stayed eleven Christmases; he knows how to lift it.'

'Oak, with the lock put in new in 'sixty-one and the one key on the master's chain. Fairbrother has oiled it every Lady Day since. It would not have wanted a poker had anyone sent for the carpenter, but the Major did not care to wait.'

'The candle boxes sit on the shelf by the back-stairs door, wax to the left and tallow to the right, as they have since Mrs. Pell's time. A person in the dark puts out a hand and knows which is which by the place. Fairbrother asks that nothing on that shelf be moved.'

'He was in it square to the desk, as he sat every night of his life, with his pen laid along the blotter. A man who has had a fright does not die tidy.' He says it to the carpet. 'Fairbrother has said that to the housekeeper and to no one else.'
'Fairbrother set the housekeeper's box square this morning. It was no liberty; it was standing in front of the tallow, and he has reached past it in the dark forty years.'
'Fairbrother has not touched the housekeeper's box. Should it be found short, she may count it aloud before the maids, as she counts other people's.'
'The housekeeper's box is the housekeeper's business. Fairbrother observes only that it has been put at the wrong end of the shelf.'

'The Major's greatcoat was on the stand at breakfast with the shoulders dry, after a night it snowed sideways on the yard. Fairbrother brushed it as he brushes it every morning. It is the Major's coat.'

'The boy sits the hall chair for the bell until the house goes up. On Thursday the boy was abed with his chest by ten and the chair stood empty. After ten, anyone crossing the hall crossed it unseen. The back stairs are another matter.'

'It is the one window on the back stairs and it gives on the yard. The snow light through it is enough to find a tread by and not enough to know a face. Fairbrother has gone up by it without a candle at all when the box was low.'

'Mrs. Ormsby keeps her door on the latch and her maid in the dressing room beyond it, only her maid did not come this year. She asked Fairbrother for the key of it the first night of the snow. She has turned it every night since.'

'Four, north-facing, with the frost on the inside since Tuesday; the master would not have the gallery fire lit for guests who were abed. From the third one can see the lodge lamp. The Major stood at the third a long while after the ladies went up on Thursday.'

'The press is on the first-floor landing and the housekeeper has the key of it now. There is a pillowslip gone from the second shelf since Thursday. Fairbrother counts linen as he counts candles; he does not say why a thing is gone, only that it is.'

'A cloth came back to the scullery on Friday morning with tallow on it and no one to say whose it was. Netherby had it in the copper before Fairbrother had looked at it twice.' He folds his hands. 'He has not asked her why. That is not his department.'

C02.history: Reginald Fairbrother came to the house as a boot-boy and has dressed the master every morning for forty years, through two wives, the nephew's schooling and the Major's long visits. On the murder night the master, who knew he was dying, told him to light the gentleman up the back stairs at eleven and say nothing of it, and he obeyed as he always has. He has said nothing for two days, and the house hired a housekeeper over his head three weeks ago, and he has not yet decided which of those he minds more.

C03.name: Nathaniel Yardley

description.text: He wears his uncle's signet now and keeps his hands behind him when you are in the room, so the ring and the yard need not be looked at together; he addresses the air a foot to the left of your cap.
Unlocked and fed, colour back in his face, he has the look of a man who has had his bet paid out on a horse he did not back; he does not meet your eye and he does not need to.

Master of the house since the hour you spoke, he stands where his uncle stood by the fire, and when he looks at you it is the look of a man counting what he owes and deciding it was the house's money.

Snow still melting out of his hair, blanket over his dinner coat, he sits on the edge of his bed with the valet on a chair outside the door and glares at the window as though the stables were a creditor.
Seven-and-twenty, too thin for his coat, a riding man's hands with a gambler's nails; he begins every answer twice and looks at the stable clock through any window he passes.

here.text: Nathaniel Yardley has the household ledger open under one hand and his uncle's signet on the other, and his back to you.
Nathaniel Yardley stands with his hands in his pockets and the air of a man who has lately been given a house.
Nathaniel Yardley sits wrapped in a blanket with his boots steaming by the fender and his jaw set.
Nathaniel Yardley is pacing with a cold pipe in his teeth, glancing at the snow on the yard window each time he turns.

says.text: 'I was on the back stair at half past ten, not eleven, whatever Evangeline recites; he said "nephew" and he said "loft" and I didn't wait for the rest.' He lowers his voice. 'What you saw crossing the yard you did not see, and we shall both be more comfortable so.'
'Abed. I was abed, damn it, I beg your... I was abed by half past ten and the valet can say so.' He pulls the blanket tighter and says nothing for a long moment. 'He can say so if he's asked.'

'I went up at half past ten, I told the Major, I told the... Mrs. Whoever-you-are, I don't see that a housekeeper's rounds need to take her to the yard window.' He knocks his pipe out on the fender though there is nothing in it.

'Four hundred at Tattersall's, two at the club, a hundred to a man I'd sooner not name.' He shrugs, easy now. 'The estate clears it by Lady Day. My uncle knew the figures; he simply wouldn't say them out loud at table.'

'Debts. Everyone has debts, Carrington has debts, he's just better at... look, a man lays a hundred on a horse called Vespers and the brute goes lame in the paddock, that is not a crime.' He laughs once and it is not a good laugh. 'My uncle thought it was.'

'Millicent has given me back the ring, since you ask, and I don't... I don't suppose a housekeeper has an opinion on that.' He turns the bare finger over. 'She knows about the loft. She's known since Tuesday. I should have liked to be the one who told her.'

'She was in the drawing room all evening, she said so, and if she... if she went up to my uncle about the settlement that's her business and his.' His voice drops. 'Her people lose money if the new will stands. That's not a thing a man says about the lady he's to marry.'
'Miss Gresham is my intended, and you'll find her a very easy mistress once this is... once the roads are open.' He stops. 'She likes her sherry at ten and a quiet house. You'll manage that.'
'Carrington has you in his pocket already, I see. Well. He had my uncle in it twenty years.' He says it to the door, not to you. 'Ask him why he came down this week. Ask him what he's owed.'

'He wants the lady for it, and he wants you to hand her to him, and he's... damn him, I beg your pardon, he's not wrong that I'd rather be in the stables than the study.' He pushes a hand through his hair. 'You read what I wrote. A man's cuff. Not mine, and not hers.'

'The Major has me at the magistrate's by the thaw. Fine. He always did lay against me.' He sulks a moment, then: 'My uncle sent for him. Did you know that? Christmas week, snow coming, and he sent for Carrington particular.'

light_on_the_back_stair.label: the light on the back stair

says.text: 'I wrote you what I saw and you put the glass on the table and said her name.' He does not shout; he is past it. 'I was in the yard with my boots full of snow and I saw a cuff on a tallow candle. A gentleman's cuff. You had that. You chose the lady.'

'Twenty to eleven, I was... I was crossing from the loft stair and the back door stood open and a light went up. Yellow, the servants' stuff, not wax.' He holds his own wrist up. 'Cuff. Starched. I'll not say it to the Major, he'd ask what I was doing in the yard. You say it.'
'He's been talking to you. He doesn't talk, Fairbrother, forty years and I've had twenty words out of him and ten of those were "Your uncle will see you now."'
'Fairbrother was— Fairbrother was brushing my uncle's coats before I was breeched. He sat at my door all night like a— damn it, like a dog at a grave. Beg pardon.'

'I owe Ashcombe a guinea from Doncaster and he'll mention it, he always does. He said heart, then he said the fire, then he stopped saying anything and wrote in that little book. A man who shifts his bet three times has seen something.'

'Evie— Miss Davenport was his favourite, if he had one. New will stands, she gets the Home Farm and I get the roof and the debts under it. She cried at dinner. I didn't. You'll have noticed; everyone has.'

'Mrs Ormsby plays whist for sixpences and wins like it's the house she's after. She sat with my uncle every evening this week, door shut, and came out looking— paid. That's ungenerous. Beg pardon. Ask her where she was; she'll tell it prettier than I would.'
'Whatever she's told you, she's seventeen and she'll say anything to keep her place, and— damn. Beg pardon. The loft was nothing. Horses. I was looking at the bay's near fore.'
'The maid? Netherby. I— I wouldn't know one housemaid from another, would I. She does the fires.' He looks at the door. 'Does she say otherwise?'

'Ellingham carried the new will down in his bag and has sat on the bag ever since like a hen. If he'd stayed in Lincoln's Inn the old one stands and I'm— well. He knows the arithmetic as well as I do, and he hasn't let me see it. Not once.'

'Quarles carries my bets to the village when the road's open and takes a shilling on each for his trouble. Doesn't mean he'll speak for me. He'd sell his mother for a dry pair of boots, and I say that fondly.'

'You can hear every door on that gallery from every other door, that's the trouble with it. Mrs Ormsby's latch, the Major's boots, my uncle's lock. I lay there counting them like— like a man counting the field at the off.'
'Staff stairs. I don't— I've never used them.' Too quick, and he hears it. 'Well. As a boy. For the kitchen.'
'He carved. The Major carved the beef in my uncle's house, with my uncle's chair empty beside him, and looked down the table at me while he did it. I'll not sit in there again under that.'
'Your room. I came in there at ten years old to steal sugar and the last woman boxed my ears for it. The keys still hang on the same hook. I expect you keep a count of who asks for them.'
'I'm not— I'm not supposed to know the way down there, and I know it better than the drawing room. Cook used to feed me when my uncle had me sent up without dinner. That's— no. That's all.'
'That's where they'll sign it. Ellingham, the Major, two witnesses, a pen, and Mrs Ormsby pouring. I'll be stood by the window like a horse brought out for inspection.'

'I was in there Tuesday twenty minutes and came out owing more than I went in with, if you follow me. He kept it locked when he was in it and locked when he wasn't. Nobody went in without him. That's— that's rather the point, isn't it.'
'The ice house? Lord. The path's a sheet in this, nobody goes near it. Quarles cuts the ice in January and that's the last anyone— why? What's in the ice house?'
'Racing calendars back to 'forty-one, that's the only shelf I ever opened. The Major sits in there now with the newspaper as if he's paid for the chair. He hasn't. Nobody has, yet.'

'I held the poker. The Major told me to and I hit the lock and it went, and I heard the key drop, everyone did. I'd not— God. Beg pardon. I'd not seen a dead man before, only horses, and it isn't the same.'

'I ran. There's no— there's no gloss to put on it, I heard "magistrate" and my legs went for the stables before my head did. Fairbrother and Quarles brought me back across the ice by the collar, and then they locked me in. In my uncle's house.'

'The dripping started before I was awake and he had the carriage ordered before I was dressed. He's very quick, for an old man. Who goes down that road and who stays is being decided by whoever he listens to, and I know whose account he's asked for.'

'Faces mine across the gallery. He leaves it open an inch, always has, every visit since I was a boy; says he likes to hear the house. He heard me, that's certain, and I didn't hear him, which is— that's the difference between us.'
'My door. Locked from the outside, with Fairbrother on a chair in front of it, in a house that's— that's mine, or will be. The key's on the Major's ring now. You'll have seen it there.'
'Oak, two inches, key on the inside. I know, I broke it. I keep— I keep going back to that key falling. My uncle never left a key in a lock in his life. He said it was asking.'
'The Major took it the first night, before the body was cold, and nobody said a word, least of all me. I'll have it carried out when— if. If.'

'One glass of sherry at nine, every night, and Fairbrother poured it. One. I asked him for a second once and he said a man who wants two glasses wants ten. The one on the desk was his, that's all I can tell you.'
'Seven at it and a chair empty and the Major carving. I counted the places the way you count a book at Epsom, and the sum came out wrong, and it's still wrong.'
'I leaned on it the night of— that night. You can see the study door from there, and the back stair door too if you hang over far enough. That's— that's just how it's built.'

'Next to my uncle's. The latch sticks and she has to lift it, so you hear it twice. I heard it twice that night, and I'll say so if it comes to it, and she'll say she heard mine. That's how a house like this goes.'
'The press on the back landing? I hid in it from the Major when I was eight. He found me inside four minutes. He doesn't— he doesn't miss much, is what I'm telling you.'
'Kitchen candles. My uncle wouldn't have tallow above stairs, he said it stank the paintings. If there's one gone from that box, someone carried it up who'd no business with the wax.'
'What shelf? I don't— I don't go in the pantries.' A beat. 'Ask Netherby.'
'A cloth. Look, I— I know nothing about any cloth. If there's something on it, I didn't put it there. Damn. Beg pardon.'

description.text: He has stopped wiping his hands. He stands with them at his sides now, as a man does who has said a thing before a witness and cannot take it back, and when you come in he looks at you first and the Major second.
He keeps himself between the door and wherever Mrs Ormsby is sitting without once looking at her, and answers the room's questions a half-second before anyone has finished asking them.
When the Major speaks to you he does not join in and does not interrupt; he studies the fire as if taking its temperature, and once, briefly, he studies you the same way.

says.text: 'I told you in the ice house and I will not unsay it in a warm room. He had three months, perhaps four, and he knew it, and he meant to put an old matter straight before he went.' He looks at the Major's chair, not the Major. 'He sent for his oldest friend to tell him so.'
'A housekeeper does not ask after a gentleman's chest.' He says it without heat, and then, quieter: 'He was not a well man. Leave it at that while the Major is listening.'
'His colour was poor. The cold did him no good and the brandy did him less.' He closes his watch. 'You will have noticed he took the stairs one at a time. Everyone noticed. Nobody asked.'
