says.text: 'I shall sign it now, and sign it true. A blow to the head, the study poker, the hour between eleven and one.' He draws the paper toward him. 'It is a worse paper than the one I meant to write yesterday, and a better one.'

'A body does not keep in a study with the grate dead and the window iced, whatever the Major thinks it is proving by lying there. The ice house is the proper place, and the certificate is mine to write.' He looks at the door. 'The sooner both are done, the fewer people have to pass it on the stairs.'
'I went out to look at the sky, Mrs. A doctor likes to know when a road will open.' A pause. 'I did not go out by the door. You may draw what you like from that, so long as you draw it quietly.'

'There is snow on a good many boots in this house. The gun room is where boots go.' He turns his cuff back, straight. 'If you are asking me where I was at midnight, ask it plainly and I shall decline plainly.'
'He was sent for at eleven. He has said he was in bed at ten.' He lets that sit. 'I have known Lucius Carrington thirty years, and I have never once seen him go to bed before the decanter was empty.'
'The Major is a man who gives orders because the alternative is being asked questions.' He says it as if reading a pulse. 'He cannot order me, which he finds very hard, and I do not make it easier.'

'Mrs Ormsby is a widow in a cold house with a dead man upstairs, and she is bearing it as well as anyone.' He does not look toward her. 'Her name is not in my certificate and I will thank you to keep it out of your drawer.'
'She takes the cold badly. I have told her to keep her fire up and her door shut.' A dry glance. 'That is medical advice, Mrs, and you may repeat it to anyone who asks why her room is warm.'

'Fairbrother knew the colour of his master's water before I did, and said nothing to anyone for forty years. If he has chosen to speak to you, you may take it he has decided the master would have wished it.'
'Forty years of another man's shirts and bedpans. He has not sat down since Tuesday. Make him. I have no authority over a valet; you have.'
'Pulse like a hare's, hands like a fish's. He ran for the stables in dancing shoes in a foot of snow. I have seen guilty men; they put on boots.'
'She came to me yesterday for a powder for the headache and stayed to ask what an inheritance looks like when it is contested. Sensible girl. She watches that boy as one watches a kettle.'
'Miss Gresham has excellent colour for a woman engaged to a man locked in his room. I note it, that is all.'

'The ward has chilblains on both hands and nobody in this house has remarked on it. She is given the coldest bedroom and the thinnest blanket. Draw your own conclusions about where she stood with the family; I drew mine in October.'

'The girl who laid the study fire. The whites of her eyes have gone pink and her hands shake on the scuttle. Somebody should tell her a fire going out is not a hanging offence, before she does something foolish with the truth to make it stop.'
'Netherby laid the study fire and has not slept since. I'd prescribe a draught if I thought she'd take it from a gentleman's hand.'
'Ellingham drinks nothing, writes everything, and has asked me three times when I shall sign. A solicitor who wants a certificate quickly has a will he wants read. That is his trade, not a symptom.'

'I have listened to that man's chest for eleven winters and it is worse each one. If Quarles says the road will carry a cart by noon, it will; he is never wrong about the ground, only about his own lungs.'

'The coldest passage in the house; the draught comes straight up the great stair. The whole household stood in it in their nightclothes while the Major swung the poker, and not one of them has so much as a cough. I find that more remarkable than the door.'
'I know them. A doctor is admitted by the front door and fetched by the back, usually at three in the morning, and he learns which treads complain. The fourth from the top does.'
'Seven at a table laid for eight, the Major at the foot addressing it as a mess, and a saddle of mutton nobody touched. I ate. Someone had to show the staff the food was not the problem.'
'Your predecessor kept it at a temperature suitable for storing butter and received me standing. You have a fire and a second chair. I noticed; it is why I am sitting in it.'

'Warmer than the drawing room, and the tea will stand a spoon. I have taken it there on bad nights when a patient upstairs wanted watching and the family wanted me out of sight. Nobody down there lies to a doctor; they haven't the leisure.'
'They keep it at a heat that would hatch eggs and sit in it saying nothing in turns. If you want to know who is unwell in this house, watch who sits nearest the fire and still shivers.'

'A north room with one grate and a window that has not opened since Michaelmas. He worked in it in a greatcoat and would not be moved to the library. I told him more than once the room would do him no good.'

'Brick, below the frost line, and dry, which the churchyard will not be until March. I have put men there before. It is not disrespect; it is what one does when the ground is iron and the house is full of guests.'

'The one room where he and I could talk without the Major correcting us on the war. He kept the brandy behind the Gibbon. I'd be obliged if that went no further; it is the only pleasant thing I know about the place this week.'

'The Major swung the poker like a man who had waited all evening for permission. I went to the body. The rest went to the window and the key on the carpet. You went to the candlestick. I saw you do it, and I said nothing, which is my habit.'

'The nephew's colour went before the Major had finished his sentence; I have seen that colour on men told a diagnosis. Then he ran. I spent the next hour getting the frost out of his feet and I can tell you the boy had nothing in his pockets but a handkerchief.'
'Dripping at dawn and Quarles at the door before breakfast. I'd have taken another day of snow, frankly. A sealed house keeps everyone where they can be questioned; a carriage at the door does not.'

'He locks it, as old soldiers do, and puts his boots outside for the boy. I knocked on it once at two in the morning for a sick man and was told to wait. I did not wait. You may tell him I said so; he already knows.'
'Locked, by habit. He is a man who likes a door between himself and the house. I do not blame him; I have one myself.'

He is quiet a moment. 'I sat outside it from midnight until the house woke, on a hall chair in a draught, because I had given her a sleeping draught and I do not leave a patient with laudanum in her and nobody on the landing. That is the whole of it, and it is more than I have told the Major.'

'A door like any other on that landing. Mrs Ormsby was sedated and asleep behind it; I will certify that as readily as the other. Anything further is not a medical question and I shall not answer it as one.'
'Two inches of oak and the key on the inside. I heard it fall as the frame went; so did you, I think, since you were looking at the carpet before the Major had the poker down.'

'Hard leather, faced to the window so he could see who came up the drive. He asked for a cushion for it in September. A man who has sat bolt upright for sixty years does not ask for a cushion without cause, and I was the cause.'
'I don't know what you keep in it and I'd prefer not to. Whatever it is, keep it locked. This household has learned to open things in the last two days.'

'I have examined it twice, once with the Major breathing on my neck and once without. Cold, as one would expect in that room; the fingers blue, the face composed; nothing I would put my name under as violence. What I think is not a column on the form.'

'Laudanum, lancet, stethoscope, and a bottle of drops made up for the master that I shall not need now. Do not let the maid dust it, and do not let the Major inventory it. Those drops are a conversation I have not finished having.'

'Warm, on account of the kitchen flue behind it. I had the nephew's wet things put there myself when we got him in from the yard. Whether anything else was already drying in it that night I could not tell you; I am not the housekeeper.'

'Tallow stinks and gutters and the master would not have it above stairs; the study burned wax, I have sat under it enough evenings to know the smell. Who would carry a kitchen candle up to that room, and why not a wax one, is a question for whoever keeps the box.'
'The slate in the ice house. I had Quarles clear it of game before we carried him down; it is the right height and the right temperature. I will not apologise for being practical about a friend.'

'The decanters were full at breakfast and a third down by dinner, and the Major poured for everyone but himself. He is temperate; it is the one thing I admire in him. Who had the rest I leave to the person who washes the glasses.'

'One glass on the desk, dry, a ring in the bottom. I put my nose in it before anyone had touched it. Sherry, and nothing else I would swear to. If you have kept it, keep it; glasses are washed in this house with alarming speed.'

C05.name: Millicent Gresham

description.text: She has stopped watching your hands. When you come in with the tray she goes on talking to whoever is nearest and takes her cup without looking at it, and the ring sits on her finger the right way round.

She sits where she can see the pantry door and the pockets of your apron, and whenever you cross the room she finds something to say to the Major. The ring has been turned stone-inward, as it is when she is counting.

She stands very straight with her hands empty, the colour gone from her mouth and nothing left of the bright voice she used for the table. Her eyes pass over you the way they pass over the hall stand.

Three-and-twenty, dark hair dressed plainly for a country house, a small sapphire on her left hand that she touches more than she knows. Her mouth is coloured a shade darker than is quite proper, and she speaks to the room in bright full sentences and to you not at all.

here.text: Millicent Gresham is at the Major's elbow, bright and talking, with one eye on your apron.
Millicent Gresham has her hands folded in her lap and her face turned to the company, and does not look round when you come in.
Millicent Gresham sits with her ring turned inward and watches whatever is in your hands.

says.text: 'I shan't ask you again. I know what I asked and I know what it was to ask it.' Low, with a glance at the door. 'Only tell me it is not still sitting where anyone might open a drawer.'
'A glass is a glass, Mrs. Hale, and a housekeeper who keeps one in her drawer rather than her cupboard will be asked why.' Her voice is bright enough to carry. 'I have said as much to the Major.'
'Is it washed?' Under her breath, while she holds out her cup for more. 'I asked you as a woman, not as the mistress of a house I am not yet mistress of. I should like to know what that bought.'

'Ten past, by the clock on his mantel. The fire was high; he had just had it made up.' She looks at the fire. 'I was there a quarter of an hour and he was alive and perfectly disagreeable when I left him.'
'I was in my room at ten with a headache. I have said so to the Major and I shall say so to the magistrate.' She lifts her chin. 'Whatever you think you saw on the back stairs was a maid.'

'If I was in the study at ten it was on a matter of settlement, which is a private thing between a family and the man at its head.' Quick and low. 'It has nothing to do with eleven o'clock and I will thank you to keep the two apart.'
'He thinks I came down here to be looked over, like a horse. He has no idea.' A short breath that is not a laugh. 'I should like it kept that way, even now.'
'Mr. Yardley is engaged to me and locked in his room, and both of those are the house's business and neither is yours.' Bright, for the room. 'You might see that his fire is kept in.'

'He saw you whisper to me at dinner. He will think it was about him; he thinks most things are.' She turns the ring. 'He ran for the stables because of it, you know. He does not run from the things he ought to.'

'Four thousand, and his uncle knew it to the shilling. I went in to ask whether a man could let his heir go to the moneylenders in the month of his marriage.' Her mouth tightens. 'He could, it seems. He said so with the decanter in his hand.'

'I do not discuss Mr. Yardley's affairs with the servants, and I did not go to the study to beg.' Her colour rises. 'Say settlement if you must say anything. I would rather they thought me capable of the other thing than of that.'
'He has been very proper. He speaks to me as if I had already lost something, which I suppose I have.' A glance toward the library. 'I do not like how quickly he has decided whose hour it was.'

'The Major is the only gentleman in this house with his wits about him, and he listens when a lady tells him a servant is not what she seems.' She does not lower her voice. 'I have found him most attentive.'

'He asks a great many questions about where everyone was and answers none about himself, which is a gentleman's privilege, I am told.' She says it lightly. 'He has his watch out at every meal. I had not thought him so fond of it.'

'I told him you pocket things. I did it because you whispered to me where Nathaniel could see, and I had to put something between you and me before he looked harder.' She does not apologise. 'I am telling you now so that you know it was not malice. It was arithmetic.'

'I told him what any lady would tell him of a housekeeper who keeps a guest's glass in her drawer instead of the scullery.' She looks straight past you. 'If your apron had nothing in it, no harm was done.'

'He poured me the sherry himself and watched me drink it as if that were the whole of what he owed me.' Her voice goes flat. 'I did not like him. I did not want him dead; I wanted him to open his cheque-book, which is a different thing.'

'A hard man with his money and a careless one with his nephew. I had not met him above three times before this week.' Bright, for the room. 'I understand the house was always kept very well under him.'

'Forty years. He still folds the master's gloves at the hall table as if someone were coming down for them.' A quick glance at the door. 'One does not dismiss a man like that. One pensions him, and Nathaniel will have to be told what a pension costs.'

'Dr. Ashcombe gave his opinion of the hour, and then gave it again differently after the Major had taken him into the window. I noticed. I was brought up to notice which way a man's opinion leans when there is money in the room.'

'Miss Davenport has been in this house eleven years and I do not believe she has once been asked where she would like to sit.' Low, over the salver: 'Whatever is settled on her, it will be a smaller sum than it should be, and she knows it, and she has stopped crying about it rather suddenly.'
'Mrs. Ormsby wears her weeds like a letter of credit. She came for the week.' A bright smile for the room, then under it: 'In my experience she stays for whatever the week can be made to yield.'
Barely moving her lips as you set the dish down: 'Netherby was on the gallery after dinner with a scuttle and no fire to carry it to. Keep her off the gallery in the evenings. I ask it as a favour.'
'Ask the girl Netherby. She appears to be the only servant in this house who can be trusted to keep her mouth shut for a shilling.'
'A soft face and hard eyes. I should not have her in a house of mine, but then it is not yet a house of mine.'

'Mr. Ellingham drew the settlement that was to be signed at Easter. He has looked at Nathaniel all through dinner as though reckoning which clauses to strike out, and he has not yet looked at me at all, which is worse.'

'I met him once, at the gate, when he would not open it until he had seen my face under the hood. I thought it insolent. I am told now it is the only reason anyone may be certain nobody came up the drive that night.'

'One hears everything from the gallery and sees nothing, which is the wrong way about for a gallery. I stood at the rail when the door went and heard the key drop on the carpet, and I have not managed to stop hearing it.'
Low, as you reach past her for the cruet: 'A lady is not supposed to know where the back stairs are. Nathaniel showed me the week we came, as a joke. I know where they are.'

'Seven at a table laid for eight, and the Major seated where he could see every face. I was placed with my back to the study passage.' She smooths her napkin. 'I do not think that was an accident of the cards.'
'I have been in it once, at night, and I shall not say so.' The words barely carry over the clink of the plates. 'Nor will you. That is all the arrangement there is between us.'
'A room with a lock and a drawer. I begin to think it is the only room in this house where things are kept rather than lost.'
'I have never been down. One does not. Though Netherby lets me understand the matter is settled there already, which is more than the drawing room can say for itself.'
'We sit and do our needlework and listen for the stairs. Mrs. Ormsby has taken the chair nearest the fire as though it had been settled on her in the will.'
'I shan't go in again. A room keeps the smell of a man after he is gone, the tobacco and the ink.' Quietly: 'If the maids talk of what the room is like now, I would rather not hear it.'
Brightly, for the table: 'I never had occasion to go into the study. One doesn't, as a guest.' Then, with the dish between you and the room: 'That will do for them. It will not do for you, I know.'

'They wished to carry him down there until the thaw. The Major said it was proper. I said nothing, because a fiancée says nothing, but I thought it was the first thing anyone in this house had wanted settled quickly.'
'Nathaniel reads there, or says he does. It is where Mr. Ellingham laid the settlement out for signing, and it is where I go now when I want a room nobody else thinks worth watching.'

'I saw the poker go in and the wood give, and I heard the key fall, and the thought that came to me, God forgive me, was not of him. It was: now it will be about where everyone was. I had already begun composing where I was.'

'He bolted before the fish. The Major had been talking at him for a quarter of an hour and he put down his fork and ran for the stables in his evening shoes.' Her voice drops. 'One does not run. It is the running they will remember, not the quarrel.'

'The road will carry by noon, the Major says.' Bright, for the table; then, as you take her plate: 'Whatever you say in the drawing room, say it as a settlement. Not the other word. I will know you did.'
'You will give your account and I shall sit and hear it like everyone else. I have arranged my face already. It is the one thing a woman in my position is permitted to arrange.'
'Dripping eaves at dawn and the Major ordering the carriage before his coffee. He has been waiting for that sound longer than any of us.'
'His door faces the top of the gallery stair. He hears everyone who passes and he says so, at breakfast, by name.' A pause over the salt. 'Which is why one takes the other way.'

'Fairbrother sits outside it on a hall chair with his hands on his knees. I am permitted to speak to Nathaniel through it. Through a door.' She sets down her spoon. 'One cannot say what needs saying through a door.'

'Oak, and the key turns only from inside. Nathaniel told me that years ago, laughing, because his uncle used to lock himself in to escape callers. I did not find it so amusing standing on the gallery.'
'I have not asked what is in it. I shall not ask.' She does not look at you. 'That is the whole of my part, and I am keeping it.'
'The Major has twice asked me whether the housekeeper keeps her drawer locked. I told him I could not possibly know.' Cool, and loud enough for the sideboard. 'I may find that I can.'
'A drawer is a drawer until someone asks for it to be opened before the room. Then it is a settlement, and everyone wants to read the terms.'

'The tray goes up at nine. Everyone in this house knows the hour the tray goes up, which is to say everyone knows when the study has company and when it has not. Nobody will admit to having counted the glasses, and everybody did.'
'Mr. Ellingham carries it under his arm from room to room and has not opened it before any of us. I take that to mean the figures are not ones he cares to read aloud with Nathaniel at the table.'
'It struck the quarter while they were still at the door with the poker. I remember thinking it very ill-mannered of a clock, and then thinking that I should not be thinking of manners.'

'The settlement was laid out on it for signing. Three copies, weighted with the inkstand. I have looked since; the table is bare, and nobody has thought it worth mentioning, which tells you who moved them.'

'Mrs. Ormsby's door stood ajar at half past ten; I passed it.' Low, quick. 'A widow's door ajar in a country house is either grief or an alibi, and she does not strike me as a woman who grieves with the door open.'
'Netherby stands beside it on the landing as though it wanted guarding. I cannot think what a linen press needs guarding from, unless it is the housekeeper.'

'I do not know what it is for. I have seen you look at it.' She straightens the cloth. 'A lady does not know where the servants' candles are kept. I am trying very hard, in this house, to remain a lady.'

'Fairbrother will not have it moved. The Major sat in it on the second morning and Fairbrother stood behind him, saying nothing, until he got up again. It was the only thing in two days I have enjoyed.'

C05.history: Millicent Gresham came to the house engaged to the nephew with a settlement her family thinks handsome and Nathaniel's creditors think thin. At ten past ten on the night the master died she went to his study alone, drank a glass of his sherry to steady herself, and asked him to pay Nathaniel's debts; he refused, and she left the glass on his desk with her colour on the rim. The next morning she found the new housekeeper and asked her, as one woman to another, to wash it and say nothing.

says.text: 'I was in my bed. The hall clock struck eleven and I heard his voice raised through the floor, and another, lower, and then the door.' The same words as at dinner, in the same order, and her eyes go to the mantel clock before she begins.

'I was in my bed. The hall clock struck eleven and I heard his voice raised through the floor, and another, lower, and then the door.' She counts the three sounds off on her fingers for you. 'You may tell the Major I said so again.'

'If your rounds say half past ten then your rounds are wrong, and I should be careful what I put in a book the Major is reading.' Her voice climbs. 'I have said eleven to the whole table. Who are you to have a different hour?'
'Eleven. I have said eleven and I will go on saying eleven.' Her colour comes up fast. 'A housekeeper's candle is not a clock, and nobody asked you where you were.'

'He took me in at six and never once sent me to a school. He said I had a good memory for faces and a better one for hours.' She smooths the black over her knee. 'I do not know who the house goes to. I only know I have nowhere else.'

'Mr Yardley's voice is low. The second voice was low.' She hesitates, which she does not often do. 'Lavinia says she heard him on the back stairs. I did not say that. I said what I heard through the floor.'

'Mr Yardley quarrelled with his uncle every visit about money, and he was the only one in the house with a reason to.' She says it brightly, like a lesson learned. 'The Major says the magistrate will see it at once.'
'He has you keeping the hours now, has he.' A small tight smile. 'He had me keeping them yesterday. You will find he does not keep two clocks for long.'

'Major Carrington has been very good. He said at once that a lady's account is worth more than a servant's candle, and wrote mine down himself.' She straightens. 'He will see I am kept on, whoever has the house.'

'He spoke of you this morning. He said you were the kind who sees without being asked, which was a compliment to you and a warning to the rest of us. I should keep in his good books, if I were you. I have taken care to.'

'He does not care for you. He said so at breakfast, over the kidneys, in front of Miss Gresham. You had better give him your account plainly and in order, the way I gave mine. He likes a thing he can write down.'

'The Major took the head of the table on the first night as though someone had asked him to, and no one said they hadn't. He writes everything in his black book. I have told him everything, in order, and he nodded at every line.'

'Fairbrother has dressed my guardian every morning since before I was born, and he does not approve of me, which he shows by leaving a small pause before he says Miss. He has not sat down since they broke the door. Somebody ought to make him. You might.'

'Nathaniel taught me to cheat at bezique when I was nine and has not improved. He runs from things. The table, the yard, the room where his uncle sat; he ran from all three and he will tell you it was something else each time.'

'Dr. Ashcombe went in first and came out and said "some hours" and nothing more, which is not an answer. I asked him for the time of it and he asked me whether I had slept. I have not. That is not relevant.'

'Miss Gresham spent her first evening asking me how many bedrooms there were and which had the best aspect. She counts things. She was counting the silver at breakfast, with her eyes, which I suppose a fiancée is entitled to do.'

'Mrs. Ormsby arrived already in black and so has the advantage of the rest of us now. She came down the morning after at a quarter past eight exactly, which is early for a widow, and asked for the fire built up before she asked how he was found.'

'Netherby cries in the linen room because she thinks no one goes there. I went in on Tuesday for a pillowslip and she told me she had been nowhere all night, before I had asked her anything at all. You should speak to her. You are permitted to; I am not.'

'Mr. Ellingham came up with the thaw and a case that locks, and he has not yet said my name without looking into the case first. I shall give him my account exactly as I gave it to the Major. It does not alter. You may test it if you like.'

'Quarles keeps the lodge and the gate, and in this weather keeps neither, since nothing can get through. He came up with the dogs at noon on the first day to say the road was gone to the hedge-tops, and after that he sat in the servants' hall drinking the household's beer. He is not a guest and he is not of the house. I don't know what he is.'

'I can give you the order we stood in. The Major nearest the door, Fairbrother at his shoulder, Nathaniel behind, Mrs. Ormsby at the turn of the stair with Miss Gresham, Netherby on the landing with her apron up over her mouth. I was by the window seat. I counted. You may check me against any of them.'

Her voice goes up a full tone. 'I do not use the back stairs. I have never used them; I am not a housemaid, whatever Miss Gresham thinks of my position here. Why do you ask me that? Who has said that I did?'
'It faces north and the fire never draws when the wind is in the east, so we were all cold at dinner and no one said so, because his chair was empty and it seemed indecent to complain of a draught.'

'It was Mrs. Pell's room for twenty years and she kept lemon drops in the second drawer for me. I expect you have thrown them out. I don't come down there. I mention it only so you know that I know where it is, and that I can.'

'I have been in the servants' hall twice in my life, once at six to see the Christmas goose and once at twelve to hide. Netherby says the talk down there is all about who was out of bed. I should like to know what they say about me, and you are going to tell me.'

'The Major has made it his court. He sits with his back to the window so the snow light falls on our faces and not his. I was questioned in the chair by the fire-screen at eleven in the morning, for twenty minutes, and I did not need to stop once.'

'I was not allowed in the study after I was twelve, when I knocked the inkstand over a deed. He kept white wax candles in there because tallow smoked the ceiling and he said he could taste it in the room. He was particular. About everything.'

'They have taken him to the ice house. I asked who carried him and the Major said Fairbrother and Quarles and the boot-boy, at four o'clock, and that I was not to go down. I have not gone down. I have stood at the garden door and looked at the path, which is trodden flat now.'

'The library is where Nathaniel and Miss Gresham sat every evening with the door half open, which is how one knows an engagement is respectable. On the night the door was shut. I noted it at twenty past ten. The Major has that too.'

'I had my hands over my ears for the poker, and then there was a small sound after it, like a coin dropped on a rug, and the Major said "the key." I did not see it fall. I heard it. Everyone heard it; ask any one of them and they will say the same.'

'Seven at the table and his chair empty. I had placed everyone in my head before the soup. When Nathaniel pushed back his chair it was eight minutes to nine by the dining room clock; I looked. Miss Gresham did not go after him. I noticed that as well.'

'The dripping woke me at ten past six. By the time I came down the Major had ordered the carriage and sent Netherby up to the study with pails. I asked why the study wanted cleaning before a magistrate had seen it and he said that was a housekeeper's question, not a lady's. So I am asking you.'

'The blue room, second along the gallery. His door was shut when I passed it at eleven. I know a shut door is not an alibi; I am only telling you what I saw, and I have told him the same and he wrote it in his own hand.'

'They have put Fairbrother on a chair outside it with a rug over his knees, as if Nathaniel were a child with a fever. He used to climb out of that window onto the leads. I don't believe he has, in this. I went round by the garden and looked up, and the snow on the sill is unbroken.'

'If you mean the Major's, it is black and lives at his elbow in the drawing room, and my account is on the third page and runs to eleven lines, and I have read it over twice and it is correct. If you mean the household's, I have never seen it. I am not shown money.'

'It seats fourteen with the leaves in, and Fairbrother would not have the leaves taken out because it had been laid for eight, so we sat the width of a field from one another and shouted about the weather.'

'The drawing room clock runs four minutes fast and has since I was a child; he would not have it altered because he liked to be early. I allow for it. When I say eleven I mean eleven by the hall clock, which is right. I made certain of that.'
'Mrs. Ormsby's is the door at the end that sticks. You hear it from anywhere on the gallery; it gives a sort of groan. I did not hear it that night. I should have, from where I was.'

'Oak, with the big brass key he carried on his chain. He locked it from inside every evening once Fairbrother had brought up the decanter, and had done for as long as I have been in the house. I knew that at seven years old. Everyone knew it.'

'The tallow is kept in a box in the still-room passage for the servants' candles. I have never opened it. I couldn't tell you exactly where; somewhere low, in the passage. Why does everyone keep asking me about tallow?'

'No one has sat in it. Fairbrother turned it to the wall on the first morning and nobody has turned it back. Nathaniel will have to sit in it eventually. I should like to watch and see whether he can.'

'There is claret at the Major's end; he spilled when Nathaniel went out and did not notice, and Netherby could not get in to change it. It is still on the table. Nobody has had the heart to dine properly since, so nobody has asked for a clean one.'

'The decanters live on the sideboard and Fairbrother counts them with his eye every time he goes past. The brandy went up to the study at ten, as it always did; I saw Fairbrother take it through the hall. That is one more thing I have given the Major.'

'The soup came round in the great tureen and was cold by the time it reached the far end, as it always is. Mrs. Ormsby sent hers back. I noticed because the maid had to go the long way round, behind Nathaniel's chair, just before he rose.'

C07.name: Cordelia Ormsby

description.text: She has her back to the glass and lets you take the pins out one at a time, talking the while of who in town keeps a good table, as though you were not there; her hands lie still in her lap, which they have not done since the snow began.

She is dressed, every pin in, and stands rather than sits when you come in; she watches your apron pocket as she talks and never once asks you to do anything for her, which from her is a kind of accusation.

The hairpin lies in its labelled paper on the table and she does not look at it, nor at the doctor, nor at you; she looks at the fire with the composure of a woman who has worked out exactly how much a servant's word weighs against hers, and is not certain of the sum.

A widow of two seasons in black silk gone soft at the seams, jet pins in dark hair that she touches when she lies; she speaks to you with the particular warmth ladies keep for servants whose silence they will need.

here.text: Mrs Ormsby has let her shawl slip and is turning a cup in her saucer, unhurried, as if the snow were a social inconvenience.
Mrs Ormsby stands with her shawl drawn close and her hand on the nearest rail, and falls silent as you come in.
Mrs Ormsby is in black silk and jet, a shawl about her shoulders, and lifts her head with a slow smile when she sees who it is.

says.text: 'I will tell you what I have told nobody, because you are the only person in this house who does not want something from me: I was up, late, and not where a widow ought to be.' She smiles at her hands. 'I heard nothing. I have come to think that was the worst of it.'

'I retired at half past ten, as the Major has written down, and I should be obliged if the housekeeper did not go about asking ladies where they were.' She does not quite look at you. 'It gives the maids ideas.'

'My dear, I went up after the quarrel like everyone else, and lay listening to the wind, and thought how dreadful it is to be snowed in with people one only half knows.' A small pause. 'You will have been on the stairs a good deal that night, I suppose. One always is, in a strange house.'

'Jet, from Whitby, the last my husband gave me, and I have been losing them in this house since the day I came.' She lets you see her count them in the glass. 'If you should find one, bring it to me and not to the Major; he would only write it down.'

'I have my own maid to see to my hair, thank you.' She touches the pin above her ear. 'Though I understand the housekeeper has been keeping ladies' pins in her apron, which seems an odd habit for a woman in service.'

'You pinned it so well for dinner that night, I remember thinking I should take you to town with me.' She laughs, and her hand goes to the loose side. 'One came out somewhere; they always do. I have not missed it.'

'There is a letter in it with my name on it, concerning credit, and a bank in town that would read it less charitably than I should like.' She says it to the fire, lightly, as if it were a bill for gloves. 'If the desk is opened before the roads are, I am finished, and I would rather you heard that from me than from the lawyer.'

'Whatever the poor man kept in his desk is for Mr Ellingham and the magistrate, and I cannot think why the housekeeper should trouble herself about it.' Her voice stays sweet. 'Unless you have been in there already.'

'He kept everyone's business in that desk, you know; letters, I.O.U.s, the little arrangements one makes when a season has gone badly.' She lets the sentence drift. 'I do wonder who has the key now, and whether they have thought what it would do to the house to open it.'

'You know, of course. You have known since the first night, and you have been kind enough not to look at me on the stairs.' She meets your eye for once. 'He is a good man in a bad position, and he went out in the snow that night for the Major and not for me, whatever his boots say.'

'Dr Ashcombe attended my late husband and has been good enough to continue his acquaintance; I hardly see what more a housekeeper needs to know.' She draws her shawl in. 'If you have been told otherwise, I should like to know by whom.'

'A very able man, and quite wasted in the country; I have told him so, and he has the grace to take it as a compliment.' She smooths her skirt. 'He keeps his own counsel, which is more than most men here can say for themselves.'

'I have said what I heard, and I said it to you in the dark, which I now think was unwise.' Her mouth tightens. 'If it goes to the Major with my name on it, I shall say the housekeeper misheard a woman in distress.'

'Miss Davenport, in the Major's room, pleading with him in that low way girls have when they are frightened, and a man's step going to and fro.' She closes her eyes a moment. 'I thought, poor child, and went on to my own business at the study door, and I am not proud of either half of that.'

'I knelt there with a pin in the lock like a housebreaker, and listened, and there was nothing: not a breath, not a page turning.' Her hand finds the loose side of her hair. 'A yard away. And I was thinking about a bank.'

'I cannot think what you mean, and I would be careful, in your position, of saying it where the Major can hear.' She rises as she says it. 'Ladies do not kneel at keyholes, and housekeepers who say they do find it hard to get places.'

'Major Carrington has been everything that is correct, and I have told him so, and I have told him too that his housekeeper asks a great many questions for a woman who came to the house a fortnight ago.' She smiles. 'He was very interested.'

'A man of the old school, which is to say he has his watch open before anyone has finished speaking and considers that a kind of justice.' She tilts her head. 'He wants the house settled before the roads clear, and I do not blame him; a house with a dead man in it is impossible to visit.'

'I know a house in Mayfair that pays forty pounds and does not read characters too closely, and I would write to them tomorrow for a woman who knows when a thing is better left on the stairs.' She says it plainly, for her. 'That is not a bribe, you understand; it is only what discretion is worth.'
'I had thought of writing to town on your behalf, but one hesitates to recommend a housekeeper who frightens the guests.' She lets it hang. 'I may write anyway; I have not decided what I shall say.'

'You are quite the most discreet creature I have met in a country house, and I said so to the Major, and I meant him to hear it.' She watches your face. 'Discretion is a quality I could find a place for in town, if it lasted.'

'Carrington is received everywhere and lent to nowhere, which in a man of his years tells one something, though I could never say precisely what. He has a gift for finding the chair that faces the door.'

'Forty years with one gentleman. Imagine it. He has brushed every coat your master ever quarrelled in and he will know which pockets were heaviest, and I would be careful what I asked him, because he answers.'

'The nephew has the look of a young man who has had his expectations explained to him in low voices by a great many tradesmen. One is sorry for him, naturally. One also notices he was the first to run.'
'You have been so very kind about the doctor, and I shall not forget it, and nor will he, which in the long run is worth rather more than my memory.'
'Dr Ashcombe attends me for my head. I imagine that is written down somewhere now, with everything else.'
'A very sound man, one hears his name in the best houses, generally in connection with somebody's nerves.' She says it as if reading it off a card.
'Miss Gresham is engaged to the heir and has had two days to watch her inheritance walk about the house looking frightened. She counts the silver with her eyes. I rather admire it.'
'The ward. One was never quite told whose. She weeps very prettily and in the right rooms, and she has been most attentive to the Major since the dinner, which is either grief or arithmetic.'

'The little housemaid with the quick eyes. She did my fire the first morning and looked at my dressing table as if she were learning it. I am sure you have her well in hand; I should want her well in hand, if she were mine.'

'The solicitor has been waiting two days for the road with a key in his pocket, and he looks at the study door the way other men look at a dinner going cold. I do hope he is made to wait a little longer. These things are better done with the family rested.'

'The lodge-keeper. I have met him twice, both times through a window, in snow. He is the one man in the county who can say when the road is open, and that is a great deal of power in a person I have not tipped.'
'It is the only warm walk in the house, and so everybody takes it, which is the difficulty. One cannot cross from one's own door to the stairs without three people knowing one's slippers.'
'You have never once told me where they come out, and I have begun to think it the kindest thing anyone has done for me in this house.'
'Yes, I know where they come out. So, it seems, does everyone now.'
'I'm sure I don't know them. Guests are not shown the back stairs, and I have always thought that rather the point of being a guest.'
'Seven at a table laid for eight, and nobody with the sense to have the chair taken away. I ate nothing and watched the Major carve, which he did very well for a man who was speaking the whole time.'
'Your little room with the fire. I came down once to ask about a hot brick and found the door shut, and was oddly glad. It is the only door in this house I have not heard open in the night.'
'I have no notion what is said down there and I would give a good deal to know, which is, I believe, the whole condition of being a lady.'
'Where we are all to be gathered to hear you, like a sermon. I shall take the chair by the window; the light is kinder there, and one can see who looks at whom.'
'You are very good not to look at me when the study is mentioned. I have noticed. One notices kindnesses in a cold house.'
'I have said I was never in it. I notice you have said nothing at all, which is a different thing, and I am not certain I like the difference.'
'I was never asked into it. Gentlemen's rooms smell of tobacco and arithmetic, and one is grateful not to be asked.'
'They have put him out there until the road, I understand. It seems a dreadful thing to do to one's host, and perfectly sensible, which is this house all over.'
'Cold, and full of sermons, and the one room where a woman may sit an hour and be assumed to be improving herself rather than waiting for someone.'

'I was on the gallery in my wrapper with everyone else, and I heard something small fall inside, a key or a coin, before the poker went through. I thought, how odd, and then I saw that yellow candle, and then I saw him, and I stopped thinking of anything much.'

'The Major stood up with his glass and made witnesses of us all, which was clever, and then that boy went white and ran, which was stupid, and between the clever man and the stupid one I knew which a magistrate would prefer. I kept my eyes on my plate. I recommend it.'
'The dripping woke me before the maids did. One lies there counting what must be done before noon and finds the list longer than the morning.' A smile. 'Packing, I mean, of course.'

'His is the one with the handle that wants oiling; one hears it from the far end of the gallery. I shan't say I heard it that night. I shall say that if I had, I should have put it down to a soldier's habits and gone back to sleep.'
'You have been most discreet about my door, and I am a woman who notices when a door is not mentioned.'
'Everyone seems to know when my door opened and when it shut. I begin to feel I should have charged admission.'
'Mine does not lock, which I mention only so that you will understand I did not lock it.'
'Good oak and a stiff lock that nobody could turn from the gallery side. It has been said so often in this house these two days that I have begun to wonder why everyone needs me to believe it.'

'The baize one. It sighs. One cannot go through it without the whole gallery knowing a servant has gone somewhere, which I always supposed was the intention. It sighed more than once that night, and I did not count.'
'I don't know it. Deal is what one has in the attics.' A pause, not quite long enough. 'Whose is it?'

'The one in the drawing room by the window. The ink is dreadful and the paper better than the house deserves. I wrote nothing at it that anyone need read, if that is the question, and in this house it generally is.'

'One leans on it to look down into the hall and finds everyone else leaning too. The night it happened there were nine of us at that rail in our nightclothes, and for the first minute not one of us looked at the door. We looked at one another.'
'It makes whoever passes it look drowned. I avoid it in daylight. At night, of course, it is simply a window one passes on the way to wherever one is going.'

'With the old valet asleep in a chair outside it like a dog. They have made a prisoner of the boy, and the boy was the only one of us who ran out of the house instead of into a room, which I should have thought argued the other way.'

'Grey all day and grey all night, with the snow heaped against them so one cannot tell whether one is watched from the yard. It is somebody's wet boots under those windows that everyone keeps speaking of, and I have very small feet, and I say so now so that you may look.'

'On the landing by the back stairs, and warm, and the one place a person might stand a quarter of an hour and be taken for a maid counting sheets. I say might. You have never asked me, and I am grateful.'
'I'm sure I don't know what a linen press looks like from the outside. One only ever sees the sheets.'

'I have never in my life had cause to know where the tallow is kept, and I should think the person who does would be worth asking. It was a yellow candle in his stick. Somebody carried that up from below.'

C07.history: Cordelia Ormsby came to the house a widow of two seasons with a forged letter of credit in the master's desk and the doctor in her bed, and she meant to leave with the first and keep the second. At midnight she knelt at the study keyhole with a hairpin, heard nothing, and went back to Ashcombe's room with snow on his boots behind her; she has since worked out that the silence she heard was a dead man, and that she thought only of paper. She cannot bear that the housekeeper might have seen her on the stairs, and so she is kinder to you than to anyone in the house.

C08.name: Lavinia Netherby

description.text: Her apron is grey with ash from the pocket down and she has not been let change it; her eyes are red but dry, and she keeps her hands folded over the stain as though that hid it. She looks at you once when nobody else is looking, and then at the floor.
She has set the pail down at the turn of the stair and is waiting, hands under her apron where there is something she has fetched you, her face turned down toward you and not up toward the gallery.
She keeps the scuttle between you and herself and answers the floor. When the Major's step sounds overhead she goes without being told, and does not look back from the turn.

Seventeen, thin as a rake handle, in a print dress gone pale at the elbows and a cap tied too tight. Her knuckles are red and split from cold water, and there is a line of ash along her jaw she does not know is there.

here.text: Lavinia has set her pail down and is waiting with her hands under her apron for you to speak first.
Lavinia keeps her scuttle on the far hip and her eyes on whichever door she came through.
Lavinia has a coal scuttle on one hip, an empty pail in the other hand, and a smear of ash along her jaw.

says.text: 'I've not touched it, ma'am. I set the pail inside the door and come straight back down for you.' Barely above breath. 'There's summat in the ash that's not coal. Yellowish, like.'
'I raked it. You weren't there.' She shifts the scuttle to the other hip. 'Cook says I'm to do as the Major bids and not stand about on the back stairs waiting on anybody.'
'The Major says rake it and have it clean before the gentlemen come up.' She looks at the stair above, not at you. 'I never done a grate with a dead man's chair still pulled to it.'

'It were me. One candle, for my room, Tuesday night, the water froze in my jug.' She twists the apron hem round her finger. 'If they count it short, say it were spilt, ma'am, say owt. Only don't let Mr Fairbrother hear it were me.'
'I've said all I'm saying about candles.' She will not lift her eyes. 'Ask Cook. She's had it out of me twice over.'
'I don't know nowt about your box, ma'am.' Too quick, and she goes red to the edge of her cap. 'Only it were that cold up top this week. That's all I'm saying.'

'He don't speak to us. He looks at your hands and then at the plate and you know you've done wrong without a word said.' She drops her voice further. 'He counts. Spoons, linen, candles. He knew that box were short before you did, I'd lay.'

'He's giving orders like it's his house already, and the young gentleman shouting through his door fit to crack it.' She glances up the well of the stair. 'He wanted that grate done before anybody else were up them stairs. Said it to Mr Fairbrother, not to me. I were just stood there.'
'They're saying the housekeeper sends a girl up to a dead man's room and stops below where it's warm.' She picks at the ash on her cuff. 'I didn't start it. I didn't stop it neither.'

'Cook's cross with the Major for carrying the master out to the ice house like a side of beef. Scullery's cross with me for the extra coals.' A small shrug. 'And they're all waiting to see who gets the candle laid on them. It's always a maid.'

'I were in my room by half ten with my—' she stops, then goes on, 'with my candle. There were a tread on the back stair after, heavier than any of us girls, and it didn't come on up to the attics.' She wipes her hands down her apron. 'I didn't look out. You don't, ma'am.'
'Abed by half ten, same as always. I heard nowt.' She says it to the pail. 'A house that size, there's always somebody on a stair.'

what_the_valet_would_say_of_her.label: what the valet would say of her

says.text: 'If Mr Fairbrother says it were me, then it were me, ma'am. That's how it goes in a kitchen.' She picks up the pail and does not look at you again. 'I'll fetch what I'm told. Only tell me, don't—don't put it to me like that.'
'Carter goes at noon. My mother'll have summat to say when I come up the lane with my box.' Ash still under her nails. 'I'll not tell them it were you sent me up. I'll not tell them owt.'
'Carter goes at noon.' She looks straight at you for the first time in two days. 'I'll tell him who sent me up them stairs with a pail. He can tell who he likes after.'
'No character, Cook says. Three winters of grates and not a line on paper.' She rubs at the ash on her apron and only spreads it. 'The Major had the stub in his pocket before I'd got the words out.'
'Mr Yardley sits up. His grate's always dead by morning and his boots is by the door where he's thrown 'em. He were cross all week, ma'am. Afore it, I mean.'

'Doctor wants his water at seven and sends it back if it in't scalding. He were the only one didn't shout when the door went. Just stood on the gallery with his hands behind him. I didn't like that better.'
'Miss Gresham leaves her gloves about and asks me to find 'em like I'd hid 'em. She were crying in the linen closet Tuesday. I went back down with the sheets and come up again later.'
'Miss Davenport's the only one says thank you. She's in the cold end over the yard and never rings for more coal, so I take it up anyhow. Nobody's told me not to.'
'Mrs Ormsby's bell goes more'n all the rest put together. Hot bottle, fresh water, the fire's smoking. It never is smoking.' A glance at the door. 'I think she just wants somebody stood in the room.'
'The solicitor gentleman come with the first snow and never got out again. He don't look at me, which suits. Only he counts things with his eyes. Spoons. Chairs. Cook seen him at it too.'
'Quarles is my mam's cousin's man. Brings the eggs when the road's open and tells the whole village what he's told at the back door. So I don't tell him nothing, ma'am. Nothing.'
'Boards go all along there. Third one past the Major's door is worst. You can't cross it quiet with a full scuttle, I've tried every way.'
'Them's mine. Nobody above stairs uses 'em, 'cept Mr Fairbrother when he don't want seeing. Dark past the half-landing when the lamp's not filled, and it in't been filled since the snow.'
'Lays for eleven and we had seven. All that silver out and his chair stood empty at the top like it were watching 'em eat. I don't go in till the gentlemen's gone through.'
'Yours, ma'am. I only come in when I'm rung for. The last one kept the key on her belt and never took it off, Cook says, not even to sleep. Cook says a lot.'
'Warmest room in the house and nobody'll own it. Everyone's cross with everyone down there just now. I eat quick and go.'
'Wants making up twice of an evening with all seven sat round it. I go in and out with the scuttle and they talk right over me like I'm the fender.'

'I'll go if you say, ma'am. I'd sooner you come as far as the door.' She lowers her voice. 'I did his grate five year and never seen him at the desk afore eight. He'd not have had the window open. Not in snow.'
She does not look up. 'You sent me. I went. It smells of chimney and of him, and I've to go in again tomorrow, haven't I.'
'I did his grate five year, ma'am, and never once seen him at his desk afore eight. He'd not have the window open, neither. Not in snow. He were mortal about draughts.'
'Down past the kitchen garden, under the bank. Cook sends me when there's a jelly and I hate it. Steps is green and the door sticks, and once it's shut you can't hear the house at all.'
'Cold as the church. Nobody rings for it, so the fire's laid and never lit. The solicitor sits in there of an afternoon in his coat, turning pages he in't reading.'

'I were on the back stairs with the hot water. Heard the poker go in, and then the key drop. Little sound, like a spoon on the carpet. Then all of 'em shouting at once. I kept hold of the can, I don't know how.'

'I were only in for the plates. Then Mr Yardley's chair went over backwards and he were out the door and me stood there with the gravy. They brought him back through my kitchen, blue to the lips, and Cook put brandy in him afore anyone said she could.'
'Dripping off the eaves afore it were light. I thought, that's the cart, then. And pails for the study.' She looks at you. 'You'll be upstairs when I go up, ma'am? Only say you will.'
'Dripping. Means the road. Means the cart.' She picks up the pails. 'Means I go up on my own, same as before.'

'Eaves started afore it were light. Cook says the road'll take a cart by noon, and the Major's had everyone running since. Pails, coal, carriage. He don't want nobody stood still long enough to think.'
'Shuts like a gun. You hear it from the kitchen. He has it locked of a night and wants his coal left outside, so I leave it outside and I'm glad to.'
'Heavy old thing. Always locked from inside when he were at his papers, and you knocked and waited and sometimes he never come. Now it hangs off and I've to squeeze round it with the scuttle.'
'Nobody's sat in it since. Mr Fairbrother turned it to the wall.' She shakes her head. 'I don't dust it. I'll do the desk, but I don't touch the chair.'
'In't my business what's in your drawer, ma'am.' A pause. 'The last one kept the candle count in hers. In a little book. I only know 'cause she'd read it out at me.'
'I'll carry it down meself when it's time. Don't let him send me, ma'am, let it be you as says.'
'Mr Fairbrother says it's to go on the cart. I'll fetch it when he says.'
'The one in your room? I've not touched it, ma'am. I don't go in your room without I'm rung.'
'I do it Fridays with the beeswax. Somebody's been leaning on it with wet hands down the study end, there's marks I couldn't lift. Snow off a sleeve, like.'
'Rattles. Snow comes in under the sash and I've a rag laid along the sill. You can see the lodge from it when you can see anything, which in't been for two days.'
'Mrs Ormsby keeps it on the jar. Says she can't breathe shut in. So you hear her all night from the landing, up and down, up and down.'
'Mine and Cook's. Warmest spot in the house, the hot pipe runs behind it. I keep—' She stops. 'I keep the sheets in there. Where else would I.'
'Decanters go on it after and the gentlemen help theirselves. I count the glasses back in to the pantry, every one. It's the only counting in this house I'm trusted with.'

'Mrs Ormsby takes one up of a night, always, and I fetch it down with the slops. There weren't one on her tray that morning.' She frowns at the floor. 'Might be she carried it down herself. She never has before.'

C08.history: Lavinia came up from the village at fourteen and has done the fires and the slops in this house for three winters, under a housekeeper who counted the tallow box loosely and did not care who had a light in the attics. She has seen two maids turned off in that time, one for a brooch that turned up later behind a drawer, and has learned that when something goes missing the kitchen looks down the table, never up. The master's death is her first change of masters, and she is already counting which of the gentlemen will keep her.

description.text: He has moved his chair so that you stand between him and the Major, and when an hour is given he writes it and turns the sheet toward you, pen out, for an initial. He never asks the Major to initial anything.

He writes with his head down and the Major at his shoulder, and the hours going onto the page are the Major's, read off a watch. When you pass behind him he turns the sheet face down, not quickly, as a man tidies.

Your hours are in his inside pocket now; his hand goes to the lapel when the Major raises his voice, and comes away again. The rest of his papers lie open on the table as if to show there is nothing else to find.

There is one folded sheet he keeps apart from the pile, under the lid of the writing case, and he has stopped writing the doctor's words halfway down it. He looks at the Major a moment longer than a man looks at an old client.

Past sixty, narrow, black coat gone green at the seams, spectacles pushed up when he listens and down when he writes. He addresses you as Mrs and not by your office, and asks what time a thing was before he asks what it was.

here.text: Ellingham keeps his papers squared under one hand and his pen capped, and does not look up when you come in.
Ellingham has his portable writing case open on his knees and a pen already inked, waiting for somebody to give him an hour.

says.text: 'A draft is not an instrument. It expresses what a man was minded to do on a Tuesday, and he was free to be minded otherwise on the Wednesday, and he died on neither.' He does not look at the writing case. 'We had an understanding on the gallery, Mrs. I have kept my half.'

'The will that stands is the one that is signed, witnessed and in my keeping, and that is the will of eighteen-seventy, in Mr Yardley's favour.' He caps the pen. 'Has anyone in this house told you there is another? I ask because I should like to know who is saying so.'

'There is a will, it is executed, and it is lodged with my firm. Beyond that a housekeeper has no need to go, and I say that without discourtesy.' He waits to see whether you will go beyond it anyway.

'He bolts when he is looked at; it is a habit, not a confession, though a magistrate may not distinguish. I should want to know what hour he was in the yard before I say more, and who has said it besides you.'

'The nephew inherits under the will as it stands. That is a fact, not an opinion, and I give it because facts are the only thing I am paid to give.' He lets the pen rest. 'What has the Major said of him to you?'

'Major Carrington is executor in all but name, and he is the master's oldest friend, and he has a watch.' He draws a line under something. 'None of those three things is evidence, and I should be obliged if you did not repeat that I said so.'

'He gives his hours very readily. I have noticed that men who give hours readily have usually fixed them beforehand, which is not the same as having lied.' He looks at the door. 'Where was he at eleven, by your rounds?'

'Your rounds are the only account in this house that was written before anyone knew there was a death to account for. That makes them worth more than the Major's watch, and he knows it, which is why he wants them in his hand and not mine.' He holds out the pen. 'Initial each hour, if you please.'

'A housekeeper's book is kept nightly and in course of duty, and a court will take it over any gentleman's recollection, provided it has not been added to since.' He turns to the murder night and runs his finger down it. 'Has it?'

'Dr Ashcombe says the master knew his time and sent for the Major, and I have written that down because I was asked to, not because I know what it is for.' He folds the sheet once. 'A dying man who sends for a friend generally sends for a solicitor the same week. He did not send for me.'

'Forty years' service is a species of evidence in itself, Mrs Hale, provided the man can say which of those years he is speaking of. Fairbrother has told you where he stood that night, I take it? Then I should like it in your hand before it is in anyone else's.'
'A valet knows what his master wore, ate, and said in his sleep, and a court will take all three from him, which is precisely why I should want to know whether anyone has asked him before I do.'

'A physician's opinion stands at law only so far as he will put his name to it, and Dr Ashcombe has so far put his name to nothing but the hour of death, which he gives with a latitude I would not accept in a lease. Has he said more to you? Doctors say more to housekeepers.'

'Miss Gresham has asked me, in confidence, what an engagement is worth if the gentleman is hanged. I gave her the only honest answer, which is that it depends on the settlement, and I notice she has since been kinder to you than to me.'

'An engagement is not a contract until it is a settlement, and there is no settlement. I mention it only because Miss Gresham is the one person in this house whose position changes entirely according to which will stands, and she knows it.'

'A ward is provided for at the guardian's pleasure, and a guardian's pleasure dies with him unless it has been written down. Miss Davenport has not asked me whether it was. I find that either very innocent or very well advised, and I have not yet decided which.'

'Mrs Ormsby's jointure is secured by deed and no will on earth can touch it, which I told her the morning after, and which she received as though I had told her the time. She has nothing to gain from any of this. That, in my experience, is what makes a widow dangerous to the people who have.'
'The widow is provided for, Mrs Hale, and provided for by instrument, not by anybody's goodwill. Beyond that I shall not characterise a client's wife to her housekeeper.'

'The girl has told you something. I can see it in the way she no longer looks at the gallery. A housemaid's word carries less than it ought before a magistrate, which is why it must be in a housekeeper's book before it is in a housemaid's mouth.'

'Housemaids go everywhere and are seen nowhere, which makes them the best witnesses in the house and the least believed. If Netherby carried a candle up those stairs that night, I should like to know which candle.'

'Quarles is the only man who knows what the road will bear and when, which makes him, for the next few hours, more important than any of us. The Major has already spoken to him. I should like to have done so first.'

'Every bedroom door in this house opens onto that gallery, and every one of those doors can be heard from every other. I have asked each guest what they heard. Each heard the storm, which is a remarkable unanimity in a house where nobody agrees about anything else.'

'I have been down them once, to see whether a man of my years could do it without a light, and the answer is that he can, provided he knows the house. That narrows the question rather than widens it. Who in this house knows the back stairs?'
'Whatever was said at that table, it was said before seven witnesses and a footman, and the Major knew it when he said it. Nothing is declared at dinner by accident.'

'Your room is the only one in the house with a lock the master's key did not fit, which I imagine you did not know, and which the Major certainly does. Anything removed from it should be removed in front of a witness and listed. I am a witness.'

'I am not welcome there and would not go if I were, but I would give a good deal to know what is said in it. The servants' hall settled on its account of that night before breakfast; the drawing room still has not.'

'It is where the Major intends your account to be heard and signed, before the whole house, so that it cannot afterwards be altered. He is quite right about the signing. He is wrong about who should hold the pen.'

'I sat in that study on four occasions this year, always with the door shut, always at his request. He kept white wax on the desk and would not have tallow in the room; he said it stank of the kitchen. I have told the Major that. The Major did not write it down.'

'He is in there because the doctor would not have him in the house and the ground will not take him, and I will say, for whatever it is worth, that no one has gone down to him since but the doctor and you. I have watched the path.'

'I have made it my office because it has a fire and a door, and because it is beneath the study. One hears a chair scrape on the boards above. I heard one that night and thought nothing of it, which I regret.'

'I was on the gallery and I heard the key fall, as did everyone, and everyone has since told me it proves the door was locked from within. A key that falls from a lock proves that it was in the lock. It does not say by whose hand or from which side.'

'The Major announced himself as the household's advocate, which he is not, and young Yardley obliged him by running for the stables, which no advocate could have arranged better. I said nothing. One does not contest a point before one knows what the other side intends to prove.'

'A road that will carry a cart by noon will carry a magistrate by evening, and whatever is signed in this house before noon goes down that road with him. I would ask you, Mrs Hale, to sign nothing you have not read twice, and nothing the Major has written for you.'
'His door is nearest the study and furthest from the back stairs, and he has said he kept it shut all night against the draught. A shut door is a statement, not an alibi, and I have told him so.'

'A man locked in his own room with the valet set at the door is, at law, a man in custody, and custody without a warrant is a thing the Major will have to answer for later. I have made a note of the hour it was turned.'
'He was found in it, facing the desk, with the pen capped, which is not how a man sits who is in the middle of writing. I do not say what it means. I say somebody capped the pen.'

'The household accounts are not my province, but I note that the Major has asked to see them twice, and a man who is interested in what a house spends on candles has usually been told something about candles.'
'There were three coats on it the morning after, two dry and one not. I did not touch them. I should have liked you to have seen which was which before the maids were sent to brush them.'
'There was blotting paper on it, and now there is not. Blotting paper is a mirror, Mrs Hale, for anyone who takes the trouble, and someone in this house took the trouble before I did.'
'It holds the old will, three letters, and a great deal of nothing, and it does not leave my hand or my bed. If it should be found open, you may take it that I did not open it.'

'Everyone leaned on it when the door went down, and so any mark there now is worthless; one cannot date a smudge. The time to have looked at that rail was before the house was woken, and only one person was walking the house then.'

'It gives onto the yard, and from it one can see the stable door and the path to the ice house, and nothing else. Whoever stood at it that night chose a narrow view. Narrow views are chosen for a reason.'

'Mrs Ormsby's door was answered on the first knock when the house was roused, and she was fully dressed. She has explained that she could not sleep for the wind. It is an explanation. I do not say it is not.'

'They were shuttered that night against the storm, and so the gallery was dark as a cellar, and no one on it could have seen a face. Every account I have taken of that gallery is an account of sounds. Bear that in mind when someone tells you they saw.'
'There were two keys to it; the master's, which fell, and the housekeeper's, which was in your keeping or was not. Before you answer, I should tell you that the Major has already answered for you.'

description.text: A broad, stooped man in a greatcoat crusted white to the knees, his beard frozen stiff and his nose the colour of a brick. He stands on the mat and will not come further in, as if the carpet were another man's field.

here.text: Quarles stamps the snow from his boots and holds his cap in both red hands, waiting to be asked.

says.text: 'Lane's open to the mill bridge, Mrs. —, and no further. Drifts past that'd bury a horse. Give it till noon and a cart might come, if the wind holds off. If it don't, you've got us for another day.'
'I heard nowt but the wind, and I'll say so to any constable that asks. Lodge is half a mile off. What goes on in this house goes on without me, and I've always liked it that way.'

'The Major walks the drive every morning like he's inspecting a parade. Asked me the first day what regiment I'd served in. I said the one that keeps the gate shut, sir, and he's not spoke to me since but to give orders.'

'Forty years, and never once come down to the lodge himself. Sends a boy with the master's orders writ out, like I can't be trusted to hear them. He's taken it hard, mind. Saw him at the yard door this morning in his shirtsleeves and he didn't feel the cold.'

'There's been men at my gate since Michaelmas asking is Mr Yardley at home. Not gentlemen. The sort with a paper in the pocket. I say I don't know, and he goes out the back way through the home farm.'

'His mare could find the way up without him. Three times before the snow this month, and the master wasn't a man to send for a doctor over a cough. Always has a word for me, the doctor. Always in a hurry, too.'
'Came with more boxes than the carriage would hold and sent the groom back to the station for the rest in the dark. She counted them off at the door. Didn't count the groom.'
He thaws a little. 'Miss Evangeline walks down to the gate most days, snow or no. Brings a crust for the dog and asks after my wife's chest. Only one up there who knows my wife has a name.'
'Her coachman knew where the soft ground is by the second bend without me telling him. That's a carriage that's been up this drive more than the once I was told about.'

'Village girl. Her mother takes in washing by the bridge. She come down to the gate crying one evening in the autumn and wouldn't say what over, so I walked her back up and said nothing. Too young for that house, if you ask me.'

'Mr Ellingham comes Lady Day and Michaelmas, regular as rent. This time he come in December with the glass falling, and a solicitor doesn't travel in December for his health. I noted it. I note things.'

'Only stairs I've ever used in that house. Yard door, scullery, up the back to the housekeeper's room for my orders and down again. Draught on them would cut bread. You hear every step on them from the yard if the door's open.'
'Mrs Pruett as was used to give me a tot in there after I'd brought the wood up. You needn't, ma'am. I'm only saying she did.'
'I take my dinner there when I'm up for the day, bottom of the table by the door. Cook feeds me, the footmen don't speak to me, and I hear more in an hour than they'd think.'

'I can see that chimney from the lodge when the trees are bare. Smoked every night of the year, the master felt the cold that bad. First light yesterday there was nothing from it. I thought he'd let it go out and gone up to bed, and I was wrong.'

'Mine to keep. I cut and packed it in January and it'll hold till August if the door's kept shut, which it isn't, because the kitchen boy leaves it. Path to it from the yard was clean snow the morning after, if that's what you're asking. Nobody'd been down.'
'I wasn't in the house for it. Cook told me, and the hall boy told me different, so I'll believe the bit they both said: the poker, and the key on the carpet, and the fire out.'

'They say Mr Nathaniel went for the stables in that. He'd never have got a horse out. Jem locks the tack room and no beast in that stable would face the drive in a wind like that one. He'd have gone the way he always goes, if he was thinking. He wasn't thinking.'

'Eaves dripping at the lodge before it was light. I waded up to say noon for a cart and the Major had the carriage ordered before I'd got my boots off. A carriage isn't a cart. I told him. He'll find out by the second bend.'

'Tallow's what we burn at the lodge, and the servants' hall, and the stables. Stinks and gutters. The master wouldn't have it above stairs, wax only, I've carried the boxes up myself. If there's tallow in that study somebody brought it there, and they didn't come from the front of the house.'

'The Major asked would the ice house take him till the road's fit. I said it's for mutton and salmon, sir, but it's cold enough. He said that would do. I'll want two men and a hurdle, and I'll want it done before Miss Evangeline's up.'

opening.text: The study door lies in two pieces across its own threshold, the hall poker beside it where Mr Yardley let it fall, and the master sits at his desk inside as though the room had simply stopped around him: window frozen shut, grate gone to ash, and in the mantel candlestick, among the white wax, a yellow tallow stub snuffed down to nothing. Major Carrington, the key that was heard to fall to the carpet already in his coat pocket, has given his order to the housekeeper, 'Below, and count the plate,' and turned his back on it to bend over the desk with Doctor Ashcombe. Fairbrother stands on the back stair with his candle held low and says, not quite to you, 'A housekeeper's place is below, ma'am, when gentlemen are in a room; the hall remembers who forgot it.' Along the gallery the guests' doors stand open and the maids crowd the stair head, and nobody has yet left the doorway the Major pointed from.

study_end.text: The broken door has been propped against the linen press. Through the gap the Major stands between you and the desk, and the mantel candlestick is behind his shoulder.
Bare boards, the fire bucket kicked over in the rush, the end window white with frost to its upper pane. The study door lies in two pieces and the room beyond it is colder than the landing.

stair_head.text: Fairbrother's candle waits at the head of the back stair, held low for a servant's feet, as he has held it for forty years of other people's.
The back stair is dark. Fairbrother has gone down with his candle and left no light behind him, which in this house is a sentence.
From the study end the Major's voice carries: '...the housekeeper will see to it.' Flat, but a title, and said where the maids can hear.
From the study end the Major's voice carries: '...that woman.' Loud enough to be meant for the gallery, and the maids on the stair hear it too.
Grey snow light through the half-landing window. The barometer has stood at Stormy for two days and the maids stand at the newel post in their nightcaps, not sent down by anyone.

gallery.text: The doors along the gallery are closing one by one, the widow's last. Mr Yardley stands on the Turkey runner with the poker he has picked up again, as if he does not know whose hand it belongs in now.
Every door on the gallery stands open and every sconce is lit; the Turkey runner is rucked where the household ran along it. The waxwings watch from their case with glass eyes.

interactions.text: The Major straightens, finds you in the doorway, and takes the excuse as he would from a footman: a nod toward the back stair, and his attention gone back to the desk before you have turned. He does not watch you go. Fairbrother does.
interactions.detail_label: 'About the fire, sir. For the doctor.'

interactions.text: Doctor Ashcombe's hands stop on the master's collar. The Major's hand goes to his coat pocket and stays there, closed over it. 'The housekeeper is new, Ashcombe,' he says to the doctor, not to you. 'She will learn what is asked of her.' The doctor does not turn round, but he has heard.
interactions.detail_label: 'The key that fell, sir. Where is it?'

interactions.text: Two steps on the bare boards, the stub cold and greasy between finger and thumb, and either it is in your apron pocket before the Major turns, or Fairbrother's eyes on the back stair go to your hand and the Major, straightening, follows them to the empty socket among the white wax.
'A sheet,' the doctor says, without turning. 'And hot water, though it will do him no good.' The Major does not look up; the stub stays where it is.
interactions.detail_label: 'Anything to be brought up, Doctor?'

interactions.text: You go down as ordered, past Fairbrother at the turn of the back stair. He is setting the tallow box square to the edge of its shelf without looking inside it, as he must have done ten thousand nights; he has counted it already, and you can see that in how he does not count it now. Below, the plate waits in its baize, and above, the keyhole.

'I will see the room, sir, before it is shut.' You step over the broken door with the key ring closed in your fist and walk the four walls while the Major argues at your back: the poker straight in its stand, the window frozen in its frame, the ash cold, and the yellow tallow stub in the white-wax candlestick, each said aloud and carried out to the gallery where the whole house is listening. Fairbrother's candle goes down the back stair without you, and the maids on the stair head hear him tell them what the new woman has forgotten.
