events.text: Mr Yardley comes along the gallery with the poker still in his hand, sets it in the fire bucket at the study end, looks at it there, and takes it up again. 'Someone should wire the police,' he says, and then remembers the snow.
The doctor straightens from the desk and says, to the room, that the master has been dead some hours, and that the window has been frozen shut longer than that.

nudges.text: Major Carrington's voice, carrying through the house: 'Housekeeper. The plate. I gave an order.'
A draught moves through the house and every flame leans with it; somewhere below, a door Fairbrother would ordinarily have shut bangs once and is still.

The morning's orders for the maids came down by Fairbrother on a folded card; your name is not on it. Your rounds book is on the cloth at the Major's elbow, fetched from your room, and he does not hand it back.

The master's chair stands empty at the head of a table nobody eats from. The fire in the grate has burned to a red cave, the portrait looks down the length of the cloth, and the snow light through the north windows has gone from grey to black.

serving_pantry.text: Fairbrother has been in here without you. The tallow box stands squared to the shelf edge the way he leaves things when he wants them seen to have been counted, and the housekeeper's drawer is not quite as you left it.
The lead sink drips. The housekeeper's drawer is shut, and whatever is or is not in it, the pantry smells of sherry and cold plate.

The plate-warmer ticks as it cools. In the housekeeper's drawer, under the glass cloths, the sherry glass with its brown ring waits unwashed. The service door lets in the sound of the Major's voice from the dining room.

interactions.text: The Major closes the watch with his thumb and tells Mr Ellingham that the house keeps good time and the housekeeper keeps it. Miss Davenport's eleven o'clock goes into the paper unchallenged, and she lets out a breath she thinks nobody sees.
interactions.detail_label: 'Wound by my hand, sir.'

interactions.text: Miss Davenport's colour goes out of her face in one piece. The Major does not close the watch. 'Note,' he says to Mr Ellingham, 'that the housekeeper disputes the house's clocks,' and the pen notes it while the table looks anywhere but at you.
interactions.detail_label: 'The hall clock ran a quarter fast.'

interactions.text: The Major looks at you a moment longer than the question deserves, then nods. The watch stays open on the cloth.
interactions.detail_label: 'Shall I bring in the next course?'

interactions.text: You run the lead sink and the brown ring goes in three turns of the cloth. You say that ten o'clock was a settlement of her father's debts and nothing else, and Miss Gresham watches the water take it and says nothing, which from her is thanks. The Major's step passes the door and goes on.
interactions.detail_label: wash it: 'her father's debts, settled'

interactions.text: She looks at the housekeeper's drawer as if it were a door she cannot lock. Then she gathers her skirt and goes out past the Major in the passage without a word to either of you.
interactions.detail_label: 'It stays while your hour stands.'

interactions.text: The pantry door opens on the Major and you put your hip to the drawer. Either it runs home and he sees a housekeeper and a guest and a dripping sink, or it sticks on the glass cloths and he sees the sherry glass and Miss Gresham's face together, and says nothing, and remembers.
She does not go. She stands between you and the drawer with her hands folded, and the Major's step in the passage comes nearer and stops.
interactions.detail_label: 'Not now, miss.'

interactions.text: Keys, thimble, a reel of black thread, and the tallow stub rolls out last and stops against the Major's hand. He picks it up, turns it to the candle, and puts it in his own waistcoat pocket beside the study key. 'Thank you, Mrs Hollis. That was correctly done.'
interactions.detail_label: turn out the apron, stub and all

interactions.text: You hold out the household book instead. He takes your word as a servant's word, which is to say he does not weigh it, and waves the book away unopened. The stub stays under your keys where it is.
interactions.detail_label: 'Keys and a thimble, sir.'

interactions.text: You lift the lid of Fairbrother's box and lay the stub among its fellows. Either the apron is empty of it when the Major asks, or the pantry door opens on Fairbrother with his candle, and he holds it to your face a long moment, and then to his box, and counts.
interactions.detail_label: put the stub back in the tallow box

interactions.text: 'Leave the fire.' He waits. The stub is a small weight in your left pocket under the keys.
interactions.detail_label: 'Shall I make up the fire first?'

interactions.text: Fairbrother is set on a hall chair square against the nephew's door with a candle on the floor beside it. The Major says, over your head, that the housekeeper walks the rounds tonight; if she brings back the house's hour she goes in the account, and if not Mr Ellingham has another word for her. You take up your lamp.

events.text: Mr Yardley's chair goes over. He is through the service door and across the yard before Fairbrother has set the carving knife down, and it is the Major and the solicitor who bring him back from the stable arch with snow to his thighs and his lips blue. The Major locks him in his room himself and gives Fairbrother the key and the hall chair.
Past midnight. Miss Gresham has been with the Major in the library a quarter of an hour, and when she comes out she does not look at you. The Major asks you to step in.

nudges.text: The Major's voice carries through the house the way it carries over a parade ground: 'Mrs Hollis. We are waiting.'
A door closes somewhere upstairs, and Fairbrother's slow tread crosses the landing to the nephew's door and stops.

opening.text: Past midnight, and the house has gone to its beds with its lies still on. You stand at the stair head with one candle, meaning to walk the rounds as you walked them that night, counting the doors against the clock; in your apron pocket is a jet hairpin lifted from the carpet at the study keyhole on your second pass. Along the gallery Reginald Fairbrother keeps his chair outside the nephew's locked door as he has since the key was turned, and he has still given you no hour for the last candle he drew; through the panel Nathaniel Netherby asks whether anyone is out there. Under the widow's door a light is burning, and Mrs Ormsby does not sleep with a light.

gallery.text: Beyond the case of waxwings Miss Gresham's door is bolted; your knock gets the bolt's answer and no voice. Fairbrother's chair stands at the nephew's door, the widow's light burns under hers.

Beyond the case of waxwings Miss Gresham's door stands a hand's breadth open, her candle still lit inside, as if she meant you to see she had not slept either. Fairbrother's chair stands at the nephew's door, the widow's light burns under hers.
Mrs Ormsby passes you on the Turkey runner and inclines her head to you, as to a servant she trusts, before her door closes on her.
Mrs Ormsby passes you on the Turkey runner with her shawl drawn across her mouth and her eyes on the wall, and her door closes on her without a sound.
Fairbrother comes out of the Major's door and holds his candle up, high, to light your way back along the gallery.
Fairbrother comes out of the Major's door, looks at you once, and snuffs his candle between finger and thumb, leaving you the dark.

The sconces are out; the Turkey runner swallows your step. Fairbrother sits in his chair at the nephew's door with his candle low, and does not look up. A line of light lies under the widow's door. The Major's door is shut, and behind it a floorboard answers its own weight.

stair_head.text: Snow still comes past the half-landing window, grey on black. The barometer has fallen since you last tapped it. The bracket lamp is out, as it was that night, and the stair-rods gleam only where your candle finds them.

study_end.text: Bare boards here, and cold. The study door is locked and sealed as the Major left it. At the keyhole, in the dust of the board, is the small dent where a hairpin lay until your second round; the master's bell above the linen press has not rung in two days.

stair_foot.text: The baize door is shut on the servants' side. On the shelf sits the tallow box where Fairbrother keeps the night candles, and above it the smoke mark of a candle set down burning. The bell wires run dead along the ceiling to the study.

back_stair.text: The rope rail is damp to the hand. At the dog-leg turn the candle streak runs up the plaster, fresh grease on old, where someone climbed with a light held too near the wall at eleven. The loose tread speaks when you reach it, as it would have spoken then.

interactions.text: You put the pin into her hand and say it must have fallen at dinner. She closes her fingers on it and says the house is lucky in its housekeeper, and you do not correct her.
You hold it up to the candle and tell her where it lay. She draws her hand back as if the pin were hot, and asks, very low, what else you keep. You put it back in your pocket.
You ask her plainly whose window Dr Ashcombe's snowy boots came from. She says she does not understand you, and her voice says she does; she looks past you at the Major's door and then stops looking.
interactions.detail_label: 'Whose window had the doctor's boots?'

interactions.text: You tell her she will take cold. She goes in. The pin stays in your pocket, unnamed, and her light stays burning under the door.
interactions.detail_label: 'You'll take cold, madam. Go in.'

interactions.text: You ask him only whether the master rang after eleven, and nothing of whom he lit. He says the master did not ring. It is the first answer he has given you in two days.
interactions.detail_label: 'Did the master ring after eleven?'

interactions.text: You tell him the heir will hear of the box at breakfast if he goes through that door. He knocks at once, twice, and the Major's door opens on your words.
interactions.detail_label: 'Go in and the heir hears of the box.'

interactions.text: You step past him and knock. If the Major opens, Fairbrother must say what he came to say before his face and yours; if the door stays shut, the valet turns and walks away from you down the gallery, his candle going with him.
You pinch the wick for him. Neither of you speaks of the door, and he does not knock while you stand there.
interactions.detail_label: 'Your candle wants trimming.'

interactions.text: You lift the lid by your candle. Eleven tallow candles lie where twelve should; the twelfth, drawn after eleven, is the one nobody has owned to. You carry the box with you.

She stops you by the waxwings, shawl across her chattering teeth. At eleven, passing the Major's door on her way to the study, she heard Miss Davenport inside it, low and pleading, and a man's step. She took it for a scene between ward and Major, and went on to listen at the study instead.
interactions.detail_label: 'What did you hear at eleven, madam?'

interactions.text: You open the box under his candle and count them aloud, eleven, in front of him, and say the heir will see this box at breakfast unless he gives you the hour he drew the twelfth. He says nothing. His hands are quite still on his knees.

You give Mrs Ormsby your arm to her door and say nothing of the pin or the letter, and she says nothing of your rounds; her key turns behind her. You pass Fairbrother's chair without stopping, and through the panel Nathaniel's voice follows you: 'You too, then.'
interactions.detail_label: see the widow in; leave him unasked

events.text: Fairbrother rises from his chair, takes up his candle, and goes to stand before the Major's door. He does not knock. He waits with the candle held low, as a man waits to be admitted.

Grey comes into the gallery windows and lies along the Turkey runner. Fairbrother comes out of the Major's door with his candle; the widow passes toward her own. Each of them, in a glance or its absence, has already decided what you are to them before the house is up.

nudges.text: Somewhere below, the kitchen clock strikes the quarter. Lavinia will rake the range at six, and after that nothing in this house is private.
Through a panel, muffled, Nathaniel Netherby: 'Is anyone still out there? Fairbrother? Anyone?'

opening.text: The eaves have begun to drip, and Barnaby Quarles stands dripping in the serving pantry to say the road will carry a cart by noon. At breakfast Major Carrington orders the carriage and tells the table, over the tureen, that Reginald Fairbrother lit the young gentleman up at eleven; Fairbrother says nothing at the sideboard, and through two floors Nathaniel Yardley shouts against his door that the old man has turned on him. The Major bars you the first floor, sends Lavinia Netherby up the back stairs with a pail for the study grate and Dr Ashcombe with the body to the ice house, and keeps you to your rounds down here until the house is gathered to hear your account of that night, before they sign.

dining_room.text: The Major does not look up when you come in. He speaks to Dr Ashcombe across you, as if you were the sideboard.
Grey thaw-light through the north windows; the master's chair stands pushed in and nobody will sit beside it. The Major has taken the head of the cloth and the carving set has been moved to his hand.

stair_head.text: The pail is gone from the stair. The wet print of its rim is drying on the tread.
Lavinia waits on the back stairs with her empty pail and the fresh scuttle, one step above the line the Major drew for you. The barometer has begun to climb; water ticks from the half-landing window.

gallery.text: The nephew's door is locked from the outside and Nathaniel Yardley's voice comes through it, hoarse now, telling the old man he has been turned. The waxwings in their case watch the Turkey runner.

study_end.text: The study door stands open on a dead man's cold. The fire bucket is where it was; the master's bell has not been rung in two days and the bare boards hold the chill.

interactions.text: She goes down white and grateful, the pail knocking her knee. The grate above is not raked, and the lie is yours to keep if the Major asks who did it.
interactions.detail_label: 'Go down. I'll say it was raked.'

interactions.text: You take the pail from her and climb the stairs you are forbidden. The study is cold and the grate is full of something that was burned in a hurry; you are on your knees in it when a tread on the bare boards tells you Fairbrother is in the doorway, and he goes down to the Major without a word.
interactions.detail_label: carry the pail up past the bar

interactions.text: She climbs with the pail held against her like a shield and does not look back. You listen until her steps cross the bare boards and stop.
interactions.detail_label: 'Go on, then. He's waiting.'

interactions.text: She sets the pail on the step and stands with her hands in her apron. Neither of you goes up or down.
interactions.detail_label: 'Set it down a moment. Breathe.'

interactions.text: She sets the pot down steady and asks, for the table, after your sister's health. You have no sister. You say she is mending.
interactions.detail_label: 'The glass went down the sink.'

interactions.text: The milk goes over the cloth. She rings for a cloth you must fetch yourself, and does not look at you when you bring it.
interactions.detail_label: 'The drawer is the Major's now.'

interactions.text: She pours as you say. The cup trembles on its saucer and the question hangs over it, unanswered.
interactions.detail_label: 'Milk first, miss.'

interactions.text: The sherry glass is still there, wrapped in a glass cloth, a dried bloom on its rim. The drawer sits a finger's width proud of its runners: someone has tried it since you shut it.
The Major folds his napkin and rings for the house. One by one they come down to the dining room, and the carriage waits in the thaw.
interactions.detail_label: 'I am ready to give my account.'

events.text: Reginald Fairbrother comes up with two pairs of boots, blacked and paired, and sets the Major's outside the Major's door and the master's outside the study. He stands between the two doors a long moment, forty years of habit with nobody left in one room to wear them, before he goes down.
Dr Ashcombe and two men from the stable bring the master down the back stairs under a sheet. The service door stands open to the dripping yard, and the cold comes through the house with him.

nudges.text: The Major's voice carries through the house: 'Housekeeper. The dining room. We are waiting on your account before anyone signs.'
Somewhere above, Nathaniel Yardley stops shouting. The silence is worse.

opening.text: The tallow stub Lavinia Netherby carried down under her apron is no longer in your box; it is in Major Carrington's pocket, and he fills the servants' hall door with his notebook open. At the long table the cook has Lavinia by the wrist, ash grey down the front of her apron, and the kitchen has gone quiet to watch. Across the passage, drawers scrape in the housekeeper's room, where Mr Ellingham is listing what is taken from you, item by item. Lavinia says it was her that took it, and looks at you.

servants_hall.text: The cook is back at her range and the long table has been wiped where the ash came off Lavinia's apron. Nobody looks at the cook's chair. The Major's boots have gone across the passage to your door.

The long table, the cook's chair pushed back, and Lavinia Netherby held by the wrist at the end nearest the hearth, ash on her apron. Major Carrington stands in the door with his book. Every face in the room is turned carefully elsewhere.

back_stair.text: Lavinia's empty pail still stands on the dog-leg turn where she set it down to listen to you. Nobody has moved it. Above, on the landing, Mrs Ormsby has stopped with one hand on the rope rail.

There is no pail on the turn; she kept hold of it the whole time you spoke, her eyes on the door below, and carried it down with her. Above, on the landing, Mrs Ormsby has stopped with one hand on the rope rail.
The candle streak on the wall has a second, fresher mark beside it. On the landing above, Mrs Ormsby has stopped with one hand on the rope rail, not coming down.

housekeeper_s_room.text: Your box is open on the iron bed and the deal desk drawers are out on the floor. Mr Ellingham writes at the desk. On the landing beyond the door Millicent Gresham stands pointing the Major to the second drawer, the one you keep locked.

Your box is open on the iron bed and the deal desk drawers are out on the floor. Mr Ellingham writes at the desk. Millicent Gresham's door across the landing is shut, and stays shut, though the Major has knocked on it twice.

Your box is open on the iron bed, the drawers of the deal desk pulled out and set on the floor in a row. Mr Ellingham sits at your desk with the inventory, pen raised. The old housekeeper's bonnet has been moved off its peg and not put back.

interactions.text: You say it to the room, not to him: you sent her for the stub and the ash pan, and it was yours to ask for. The Major turns a page and writes your name below hers, in the same hand. The cook lets go of Lavinia's wrist as if it had gone hot.
interactions.detail_label: 'I sent her up. The stub was mine.'

interactions.text: You take Lavinia by the elbow, walk her past the Major and across the passage, and shut the kitchen door on the cook's open mouth. In your room she gets a chair and a clean apron from your box. The kitchen talks of you instead, for the rest of the day.
interactions.detail_label: take her into your room, shut the door

interactions.text: You stand where staff stand and say nothing. The cook finishes. Lavinia is given her notice at the table with the ash still on her apron, and does not look at you again.
interactions.detail_label: say nothing; let the cook finish

interactions.text: The Major considers you, then the girl, and shuts his book without writing. 'Nobody leaves this floor,' he says, and goes across to Ellingham. The cook keeps hold of the wrist.
interactions.detail_label: 'Finish your list first, Major.'

interactions.text: Ellingham looks at the jet head of the pin, then at you, and writes 'one hairpin' and nothing after it. On the landing the widow's hand leaves the rail and her step goes away upward.
interactions.detail_label: 'A lady's. I could not say whose.'

interactions.text: You name it: Mrs Ormsby's, found at the study keyhole on the stroke of midnight. Ellingham writes it all, the hour included, and the Major turns his head to the landing. Cordelia Ormsby goes to Dr Ashcombe's door without a word and does not come out.
interactions.detail_label: 'Mrs Ormsby's, from the study keyhole'

interactions.text: You say nothing of the pin. You take your rounds book from under the account book and hold it out to the Major before he can find it himself. He takes it as if it had always been his and tells Ellingham to list it last.
Ellingham sets the pin on the blotter beside his inventory and goes on with the drawers. The Major stays in the door. The pin sits there, black on white, waiting.
interactions.detail_label: 'Count the rest first, sir.'

interactions.text: The box is two stubs short of the count in your account book, and the lid has a grey thumbprint on it that was not there this morning. Someone has been to the box since Lavinia came down.
You push through the baize into the cold of the front hall, where the snow light is grey through every window and the Major's voice is already carrying from above.

events.text: Major Carrington shuts his notebook, steps out of the servants' hall and crosses to the housekeeper's room, where Mr Ellingham's pen has stopped over something small and black.
From the housekeeper's room, the scrape of a drawer pulled clean out and set down on the boards. Ellingham's voice: 'And this one is locked, Major.'

nudges.text: Mr Ellingham's voice, dry, carrying along the passage: 'The housekeeper, if you please. There is an item here I am not able to name.'
The cook's voice reaches every corner of the lower house: 'Ash on her, plain as print, and nobody to speak for her.'

opening.text: The drawing-room fire has been built high, as it was at ten on the night the master died, and the eight of them are arranged before it like a jury that has already voted. Major Carrington holds a sheet of his own writing out towards you and says, without looking at you, that the housekeeper will read it to the room so that the matter is closed before the roads open. On the sofa table lies the candle box, its lid shut, and beside it a twist of paper labelled in Mr Ellingham's hand. Fairbrother stands by the double doors with his hands at his sides, and the snow light through the tall windows is grey on every face.

drawing_room.text: The Major holds his written account out to you himself, as one hands a paper to a person who can read it, and waits.
The Major has given his paper to Mr Ellingham, who reads it aloud over your head as though you were the hearthrug. You are to stand there and be the proof of it.
Mrs Ormsby sits beside Dr Ashcombe on the sofa, close enough that their sleeves touch; she has not taken her eyes off the hairpin in its paper.
Mrs Ormsby has taken the window seat, the whole width of the room between herself and the doctor, and the snow light makes her look already in mourning.
The fire is high and the coal scuttle nearly empty. The mantel clock, which nobody has wound, has stopped at twenty to twelve.

front_hall.text: At the foot of the back stairs Lavinia holds the baize door open for you with her shoulder, and lowers her eyes, and says nothing, which from her is a great deal.
The baize door at the foot of the back stairs swings shut in your face. Lavinia's heels are already on the servants' stair.
Snow has drifted against the inside of the front door where it does not fit its frame. The hanging lantern is still lit from last night; no one has thought to put it out.

interactions.text: You say that Miss Gresham went to the study at ten to ask the master, plainly and as one asks a thing of a relation, to settle her father's debts, and that the sherry was his and not hers. Nathaniel's face closes like a book, but it does not break. Millicent keeps her chin level and looks at the fire.
interactions.detail_label: 'Her father's debts, asked plainly'

interactions.text: You say she begged. You say it in the voice one uses for the inventory. Millicent stands as if she had been struck, and the glass of the thing is in the air between her and Nathaniel, and he does not go to her.
interactions.detail_label: 'She begged him, over a glass'

interactions.text: You say the glass will keep, and turn back to the box. Millicent lets out a breath nobody but you hears. Nathaniel does not stop looking at her.
interactions.detail_label: 'The glass can wait. The candles first'

interactions.text: You say that as far as you saw the gallery was empty at midnight, and you saw a good deal. The doctor nods once, uncaps his pen, and signs. Across the room the widow's breath goes out of her slowly, like a kettle taken off the hob.
interactions.detail_label: 'The gallery was empty at midnight'

interactions.text: You say Mrs Ormsby knelt at the keyhole at midnight and went afterwards to the doctor's own door. The pen does not pause; he signs anyway. But he does not look at her, and he does not offer her his arm, and you understand he will not until the carriage.
interactions.detail_label: 'Mrs Ormsby knelt there at midnight'

interactions.text: You say the certificate is his business and the gallery yours, and he may ask again when the ink is dry. He holds the pen above the paper. Mrs Ormsby's hands are white on the hairpin's wrapper.
interactions.detail_label: 'Ask me after you have signed, Doctor'

interactions.text: You say nothing. The fire ticks. The silence goes on long enough for a man to decide what forty years were for, and then Fairbrother says, to the room and in his own words, that he lit the Major up the back stair at eleven, and stood at the master's door, and heard the key turn behind him.
You say that Fairbrother lit the Major up the back stair at eleven, and tell him to confirm it. He says 'yes' to the carpet. The room has heard your word and not his, and he knows it, and so do you.
interactions.detail_label: 'You lit the Major up at eleven'

interactions.text: You ask him for coal, as you would on any evening. He goes to the scuttle and finds it nearly empty, and kneels to scrape it anyway, and the room waits while he does.
interactions.detail_label: 'Fairbrother, more coal on the fire'

interactions.text: You lift the lid and count in the voice you use for the linen: eleven white candles, and one slot empty. You say that a key in a lock fills its keyhole, and that at midnight you saw the lamp through the master's. Which means the key was not in it. Mr Ellingham sets down the Major's paper very quietly.

You say his name, and nothing after it, because nothing after it is needed. The Major's hand goes to the mantel. Nathaniel Yardley takes one arm and Mr Ellingham the other, and the fire, built high as it was at ten, throws their shadows across the double doors.
interactions.detail_label: 'Major Carrington.'

events.text: Dr Ashcombe clears his throat and says, to the fire rather than to anyone, that the master's summons reached him at ten past eleven, and that when he went up the Major was already coming down.
The stopped mantel clock gives one dry click as its spring lets go. Evangeline Davenport flinches; the Major does not.

nudges.text: The Major's voice, carrying through the house: 'Read it. The woman was engaged to read it, not to stand there.'
Somewhere a door the snow has swollen groans in its frame, and nobody moves to see, because everyone is listening for what you will say next.

opening.text: The thaw has come overnight and the house drips from every gutter; the drive is black slush and the first cart stands at the kitchen door. On the stair head Major Carrington buttons his coat with your rounds book, the stub and the study key in his breast pocket, Mr Ellingham beside him saying which of it will stand before a magistrate. Mr Yardley, master since the reading of the will, has pressed a second key into your hand and gone to wait at the study end, and below you Mr Fairbrother is carrying forty years down the back stairs in one box, the lid tied with cord. Lavinia Netherby comes behind him with hers.

stair_head.text: Miss Gresham comes down past you with her chin up and her gloves on, the ring no longer on her hand. She does not look at Mr Yardley and she says nothing to the solicitor of why. Grey snow light through the half-landing window; the barometer has begun, at last, to climb.

Miss Gresham stops at the newel post beside Mr Ellingham and speaks low, and you catch 'the housekeeper's drawer' before she sees you and finishes the sentence anyway. The barometer has begun to climb. The snow light is the same grey it has been for three days.
Meltwater ticks past the half-landing window. The barometer needle has moved for the first time in three days. The Major's gloves lie on the newel post, waiting for his hands.

gallery.text: Mrs Ormsby comes along the Turkey runner on the doctor's arm, slow, and passes the Major's man at the sconce without a word or a glance. The widow's door stands open behind her on a stripped bed.

Mrs Ormsby pauses on the doctor's arm by the Major's man and says, as if of the weather, 'The housekeeper's apron was very full that night, I thought,' and goes on. The widow's door stands open behind her on a stripped bed.
The sconces are out. The case of waxwings has been turned to the wall by someone packing. Three doors stand open on three stripped beds.

stair_foot.text: The tallow box is squared on its shelf, its lid down, its edge exactly to the edge of the board, the way it was kept for forty years. Mr Fairbrother's box stands by the baize door with its cord tied in a valet's knot.

The tallow box lies where you left it, lid askew, a stub rolled against the pail hook. Mr Fairbrother has looked at it and left it. His own box stands by the baize door with its cord tied in a valet's knot.
The smoke mark above the shelf is the only thing here that has not been packed or carried. Through the baize door, the carter's horse shifts in its harness.

back_stair.text: The lower flight is quiet. The candle streak on the wall has dried to nothing and the loose tread does not creak under an empty house.
Lavinia Netherby stands at the dog-leg turn with her box against her hip, waiting for you to pass. She does not speak. Her eyes go to the candle streak and away.

study.text: The fire is out and the fender cold. The reading lamp has been emptied, the tantalus locked, the tallow drip scraped from the writing table by someone who did not do it well. The inside lock gleams where the Major's man oiled it for his notes.

study_end.text: Mr Yardley waits at the end window with his back to the study door, looking down at the drive. The master's bell hangs still on its wire. The bare boards show where the fire bucket stood for two days and stands no longer.

interactions.text: He does not look up from the Major's pocket. 'Your rounds book stands. The stub stands with it. The key stands if the Major says where it was found and you say when.' He closes the Major's coat over it himself. 'The rest is a house talking, and houses are not sworn.'
interactions.detail_label: 'What will stand, sir?'

interactions.text: He takes up his box as if it weighed nothing, which after forty years it does. Lavinia comes down the last flight behind him without a word and the two boxes are roped on the cart's tail together. What he says to the carter, you do not hear; the baize door swings shut on it. The back stairs are quiet.
interactions.detail_label: 'The carter is waiting, Mr Fairbrother.'

interactions.text: He does not turn from the window. 'Locked. Until the spring, at least. I shan't use it.' A pause. 'You saw where everyone was. You'll have seen where I was.' He waits for you to answer and you do not, and he nods as if that were the answer.
interactions.detail_label: 'Is it to be kept locked, sir?'

interactions.text: The carriage is gone down the thawing drive and the cart after it. The new master's key turns in the lock with the small clean sound the old one made from the inside. You stand with it warm in your hand and an apron with nothing in it; the house is quieter by four people, and the master's name went down the drive with them.

events.text: Wheels grind on the gravel below. Major Carrington and Mr Ellingham are gone down the drive with what the house has decided, and the half-landing window shows only slush and two black ruts.

nudges.text: Somewhere below, the carter's horse stamps and the harness rings. The first cart will not wait on the house.
Mr Yardley's voice, carrying along the gallery: 'The study, when you have a moment. I should like it locked before dark.'

opening.text: Dawn, and the eaves have begun to drip; Barnaby Quarles has waded up from the lodge to say the road will carry a cart by noon, and the Major has ordered the carriage and sent Lavinia up the back stairs with two pails and a fresh scuttle to lay the study fire alone. He halts you at the gallery rail with his watch open and says, low, that the sherry glass in your drawer with a lady's mouth on it is evidence or it is blackmail, and the drawing room will hear from you of a visit at ten and the quarrel after, or the heir will hear which it is. Below, Mrs Ormsby, whose hairpin and whose letter you kept last night for the price of her whisper, leans dressed and languid against the newel and tells him his housekeeper is the most discreet creature she has met in a country house. Mr Fairbrother was never asked his hour and has not offered it; from behind the nephew's door a pencilled scrap slides out onto the Turkey runner, and Nathaniel's voice through the panel: so you have left me to it too.

stair_head.text: Melt-water ticks against the half-landing window. Mrs Ormsby's hand is closed on the newel post and she watches the gallery, not you.
Lavinia has set her pails down on the turn of the back stair and stands straight, the scuttle handle still swinging, waiting to see if you will come.
Lavinia keeps the scuttle between you and herself on the turn of the back stair and does not look up.

Melt-water ticks against the half-landing window and the barometer has climbed a hair. Barnaby Quarles stands dripping on the bottom step with his hat in his hands; Mrs Ormsby leans at the newel; Lavinia waits on the turn of the back stair with coal and two pails.

gallery.text: The Major has turned his back to the rail. His watch is open in his palm and he does not look at you as you pass; behind the nephew's door a chair scrapes and goes still.
The Major nods you along the rail as a man nods a sergeant past, watch open, counting. Behind the nephew's door a chair scrapes and goes still.
The Major stands at the gallery rail with his watch open, the snow light grey on the case of waxwings. A folded scrap lies on the Turkey runner at the foot of the nephew's door.

study_end.text: The study door is shut. From behind it, the scrape of a shovel on the grate and the knock of a pail set down on the hearth.
The study door stands ajar on bare boards. Inside, the grate still holds its ash from the night the master died; the scuttle has not yet come.

interactions.text: She sets the pails down on the turn and waits, hands folded on the scuttle. Above you the Major does not close his watch, and the cart's hour runs on while he keeps you at the rail.
interactions.detail_label: 'Wait. I'll come in with you.'

interactions.text: She goes up past you with the pails and the study door shuts on her and the ash. You keep your place beneath the Major's watch, and he sees that you keep it.
interactions.detail_label: 'Go on in. Lay it as you were told.'

interactions.text: You go up past her and through the study door and have the ash pan in your hands when the Major's voice comes down the gallery after you. Whether it halts you at the grate or on the threshold, Lavinia has seen you come for her, and he has seen you climb.
She minds them. She does not go up and she does not set the pails down, and the water in them trembles with the drip from the eaves.
interactions.detail_label: 'Mind the stair-rods with those pails.'

interactions.text: You curtsey and say it. She inclines her head a quarter inch; the hairpin and the keyhole are closed between you, and the Major, hearing nothing in it, snaps his watch half shut.
interactions.detail_label: 'The carpet was swept clean, madam.'

interactions.text: Her hand closes on the newel post. The Major's eyes go from her to you and stay there, and the watch in his palm is forgotten for the first time this morning.
interactions.detail_label: 'Did you sleep at all, madam?'

interactions.text: 'So I hear,' she says, and goes on looking at you with her palm open on the newel, waiting still for what you will do with her praise.
interactions.detail_label: 'The carriage is ordered, madam.'

interactions.text: You stoop as if to straighten the runner and the scrap goes into your apron. Behind the panel, the nephew's breath lets out.

Behind the linen press door, out of the gallery's sight, you unfold it: pencil pressed hard enough to tear. Yard, twenty to eleven; one light going up the back stair, servants' tallow by the colour; a man's cuff on it, not a sleeve. Tell them. The hand that carried the stub was never a lady's.
The Major closes his watch. 'Then we'll have it before the papers,' he says, and stands aside from the rail to let you go down first, so that the drawing room sees you come in ahead of him.
interactions.detail_label: 'I'll come down and give my account.'

events.text: Through the end window, the carriage horses are being put to in the yard; the ring of a hoof on cleared stone carries up the well, and below, the drawing room door opens on a murmur that stops when it hears the stair.
Barnaby Quarles, from the bottom step, to no one: the lane is running clear to the turnpike, and he will not answer for the bridge past one.

nudges.text: Somewhere above you a watch-case clicks shut and open again. The house has a clock this morning that is not its own.
Lavinia's voice, carried along a passage: the pails are getting cold, and Mr Carrington says the papers are laid out and waiting on the housekeeper.

opening.text: The ice house is colder than the yard, and the snow light comes grey through the open door onto the slab where Gideon Ashcombe has laid the master under a sheet. Cornelius Ellingham has his writing case open on the ice stack, and the doctor has just said, flat as weather, that the master knew he was dying and had sent for his oldest friend; the pen waits on the next thing. Up at the house the study grate is relit, the tallow stub gone out with the ash, and word has come down that Lavinia Netherby is at the servants' hall table telling the cook she was left to the study alone.

ice_house.text: Mrs Ormsby's own maid comes wading down the yard with your shawl over her arm, sent by her mistress, and stands in the doorway not looking at the slab.
Nobody comes down from the house. Your skirts have frozen stiff at the hem and crack when you move.
The drain ticks as the ice stack sweats. Chalk marks on the slab show where the doctor has measured; the sheet does not quite cover the master's feet.

servants_hall.text: Lavinia sees the snow on your skirts and moves up the bench without a word, making room beside her at the long table.
Lavinia sees you in the doorway, turns her shoulder, and goes on talking to the cook as if the draught had come in alone.
The kitchen goes quiet when it sees you. Lavinia's hands lie on the long table grey with ash to the wrist. Fairbrother stands at the dresser counting lamps.

drifted_yard.text: Your own trench runs from the area door to the ice house. A second line of prints crosses it from the gun room side, already softening at the edges, and ends at the pump.

interactions.text: You say a housekeeper does not know what ladies know. The doctor nods as if that were the whole answer and bends back to the body. Ellingham writes two words and stops. The keyhole at midnight stays yours.
interactions.detail_label: 'The boots and window are all I know.'

interactions.text: You tell him she heard the ward turn in the Major's door on her way there. Ellingham's pen goes the length of a line without lifting. The doctor says, in the voice he uses for weather, that he will have to put it to her.
interactions.detail_label: 'She was at the keyhole at midnight.'

interactions.text: You wade back up your own trench to the gun room. Either you come down again with the boots under your shawl and the doctor turns them to the grey light, the dried tide line white across the ankle, and Ellingham writes without being told; or the groom is standing over them with the Major's orders and you come down with your arms empty and your face hot. Either way the kitchen window had you crossing the yard with the Major's things.
You draw the sheet down over the master's feet and straighten it. The doctor waits. Ellingham waits. The drain ticks.
interactions.detail_label: 'Let me make him decent first.'

interactions.text: You say it to the whole table, that whatever went out with the ash went out on your order. The cook's eyebrow goes up and the kitchen will carry it to the Major by dinner. Under the table, Lavinia's hands stop shaking.
interactions.detail_label: 'I sent her to the grate alone.'

interactions.text: The kitchen turns back to her as one. The cook says what kitchens say about girls who do not wait, and Lavinia looks at her grey hands and says nothing.
interactions.detail_label: 'She was told to wait on the landing.'

interactions.text: You take the cup from the dresser and drink it standing, and set it down, and go to the stair. The talk starts again behind you before the door is shut.
She gets up to fill the can. The kitchen watches her go and watches you, and decides nothing yet.
interactions.detail_label: 'Hot water for the doctor, Netherby.'

interactions.text: They come from the gun room door, not the area, and someone has been to the pump and back since the snow stopped. At the pump the handle is clear of snow and the trough beneath it is pink with what has been rinsed off.
You go up the back stair with the house gathering above you. Lavinia is ahead with the lamps, and either sets a lit candle at your elbow before you have asked or leaves you to find your own light.

events.text: Fairbrother sets the last lamp on the dresser and says, to no one, that the drawing room is laid: the master's chair drawn to the fire for the Major, the sherry decanter taken from the sideboard, the pale ring left where it stood. Forty years of service, turned in an afternoon toward whoever sits at the head. He sends Lavinia up with the lamps.

nudges.text: Somewhere above, the dressing bell rings early. Fairbrother has rung it for the hearing, and the house will not wait on the ice house or the kitchen.
The cold has got into your hands; the pen and the kitchen and the Major are each waiting on what you will say, and none of them will wait long.

opening.text: The name has been said, and the drawing room has emptied of everyone it did not need. Major Carrington keeps his seat at the sofa table with Ellingham's pen uncapped beside him and his own watch laid face up on the page, and the fire is burning low. Through the double doors, Miss Gresham stands in the front hall under the hanging lantern waiting for a cloak nobody has yet brought, a heavy greatcoat on the stand beside her with one pocket dragged down by the wrapped sherry glass. Fairbrother waits at the foot of the stair with Mr Yardley's door key flat on his palm, not yet turned.

drawing_room.text: The widow has drawn her chair to the Major's side with her fan up, so that whatever she says to him passes behind it. The sherry glass is gone from the sofa table; the ring it left is drying.
The widow sits apart with her hands folded, watching you as a woman watches a servant she has decided to keep. The sherry glass is gone from the sofa table; the ring it left is drying.
The Major has the solicitor's page turned so that you must read it upside down from where you stand. He has not asked you to sit.
The Major has set a chair at the sofa table for you, which he has not done for staff before, and turned the page to face it.
The page is sanded and gone into Ellingham's pocketbook; the watch is back in the Major's waistcoat. The fire wants coal and nobody has rung for it.
The fire is low and the moderator lamp has been turned up against the grey from the windows. The sherry glass is gone from the sofa table; the ring it left is drying.

front_hall.text: Miss Gresham waits with the front door at her back. The greatcoat on the stand is buttoned to the collar over whatever it carries, and the lantern has begun to gutter.

The Major's greatcoat sags on the coat stand, one pocket weighted. Miss Gresham stands under the hanging lantern with her back to the room, cloakless, and does not turn when the boards speak under you. Snow light lies on the card salver.

interactions.text: He answers the question you asked: a tray, he thinks, and the small claret. Then he goes up and you hear the key turn on the landing. The hour stays his.
interactions.detail_label: 'Dinner, or a tray sent up?'

interactions.text: 'The stair was dark by eleven,' he says, which is not what you asked. He does not move toward the landing. The key lies flat on his palm until you have gone, and only then do you hear it turn.
interactions.detail_label: 'When did you light the Major up?'

interactions.text: 'The box is mine to count,' he says, not loudly. 'I counted it before you came to this house.' He closes his hand on the key and goes up without looking back at you.
interactions.detail_label: 'The box was one candle short.'

interactions.text: He inclines his head and reaches for the lantern with his free hand. The key stays flat on the other palm, waiting.
interactions.detail_label: 'The hall lamp wants trimming.'

interactions.text: She turns and looks at you for the first time since the drawing room. She says nothing, but her hands, which have been holding each other, let go.
interactions.detail_label: 'Ten o'clock was a settlement.'

interactions.text: You bring the cloak down and put it over her shoulders. She lets you do it as if you were a hook on the wall, and fastens the clasp herself.

You have the wrapped glass in your apron when his step sounds on the stair, and must set it back in the pocket under his eye; or his hand is on the coat before yours and he buttons it to the collar, saying your surname once. Either way Miss Gresham has seen you reach, and will not forget it.
interactions.detail_label: the greatcoat: take out the glass

interactions.text: 'No,' she says to the door. The greatcoat goes on sagging, and the question she asked you hangs in the cold of the hall unanswered.
interactions.detail_label: 'The carriage is not round yet.'

interactions.text: You read it back as he gave it: eleven by his watch, the lady's candle, nothing of the key. 'That is how the house remembers it,' you say. He nods to Ellingham and the page is sanded.
interactions.detail_label: read it back as dictated: eleven

interactions.text: You read half past ten where he has eleven, and the back stair dark by eleven. Ellingham's pen stops. 'The housekeeper is tired,' the Major says to the page, not to you. 'It stands as dictated.' The sand goes on over your correction.
interactions.detail_label: read back half past ten instead

interactions.text: 'The carriage will wait on the page,' he says. Ellingham's pen stays wet above the paper, and the watch goes on ticking face up between you.
interactions.detail_label: 'Shall I see to the carriage first?'

interactions.text: You open the front door on the cut road and the steaming horses, and stand on the step as the house expects you to while Miss Gresham is handed up. Nobody looks back at the windows.
interactions.detail_label: see Miss Gresham to the carriage

events.text: Boots on the front step and a stamp of hooves: the groom has brought the carriage round, and the horses stand steaming in the snow light beyond the door.
Above, a door is tried from the inside and found locked, twice, and then left alone.

nudges.text: The Major's voice carries through the house: your surname, once, and then the word 'carriage'.
Somewhere the mantel clock strikes the quarter, and the hall lantern gutters and steadies; the horses will not stand much longer in this cold.

opening.text: The thaw has come and the front door stands open on a road running with meltwater; the carriage waits at the step with Major Carrington already up on the box, the wrapped sherry glass buttoned inside his coat. Millicent Gresham is on the threshold in her travelling dress, her trunk corded behind, and Nathaniel Yardley has just come down past her for the stables without turning his head. From the drawing room, through the double doors, Evangeline Davenport's voice gives Mr Ellingham her eleven o'clock again, word for word; from the dining room comes the small sound of Fairbrother laying the sideboard. The house is yours to see off and shut up, and nobody has rung.

front_hall.text: Miss Gresham stops on the front step with the carriage door open and the wet road behind her, and turns back to you. 'I asked you as a woman,' she says, low, so the Major on the box will not hear. 'I shall remember that you answered as one.' Then she goes down.

Miss Gresham goes out to the step without her cloak, though the wind is coming up the drive with the thaw in it, and her eyes pass over you on the way as they pass over the hall chair and the coat stand.
The front door stands open on grey light and dripping. Meltwater runs in the ruts of the drive; the hanging lantern is out and nobody has thought to light it. The carriage waits at the step.

dining_room.text: Fairbrother has your tea things set out at the end of the sideboard, the linen folded in thirds the way you asked for it your first week, which nobody in this house has done before without being told twice.
Fairbrother stands behind your chair at the sideboard where you cannot see his face, and stays there, and says nothing about the hour.

The Major carves in the master's chair as if it were his own mess table. When the plates are gone he draws the study key off his chain and slides it across the drawn cloth between the candlesticks, on his open hand, and speaks your surname to the room. 'The house is in good hands.'

The Major carves in the master's chair and does not look down the table. The study key stays on his chain; it catches the candlelight when he reaches for the salt. He has not spoken your name since the carriage went.
The cloth is drawn, the candles lit against a north window gone the colour of pewter. The master's chair is pulled out from the head of the table. The portrait watches it.

serving_pantry.text: Lavinia has brought your tea unrung and set it on the housekeeper's table, steam standing up in the cold. She lingers at the service door. 'Grate's relit in the study,' she whispers. 'And nobody has asked about my candle. Nobody at all.'
Lavinia sets the tea down on the housekeeper's table without a word and goes out by the service door, and does not look back to see whether you drink it.
The lead sink drips. The glass cloths hang in their row, and the housekeeper's drawer is shut on the rounds book. A cup of tea stands on the table, going cold.

study.text: The grate has been relit and the room smells of coal instead of tallow. The reading lamp is dark; the drip on the writing table has been scraped away and the wood oiled over it. The inside lock is whole. Nobody broke it.

drawing_room.text: Miss Davenport sits in the window seat with the work basket on her knee and tells Mr Ellingham, again, that the clock had just struck eleven. He does not write it down this time. The mantel clock ticks on toward dinner.

interactions.text: She inclines her head the exact degree a lady gives a housekeeper, and gets up into the carriage. The Major shakes out the reins. The wheels take the meltwater with a sound like torn cloth, and the road has her.
interactions.detail_label: 'A safe road, Miss Gresham.'

interactions.text: You drink it standing, in the cold, with the sink dripping. It is the first thing anyone in this house has brought you without a bell.

You go up with the last candle and lock the study door, with the Major's key or at his elbow while he turns his own. Behind you Fairbrother comes down the back stairs with the tallow box, counts it without looking, and either bids you goodnight by your name or lets the dark carry the hour away with him. The key turns in a lock nobody broke.
interactions.detail_label: up to lock the study for the night

events.text: The front door is shut at last and the hall goes dim. Through the glass the carriage is a small dark shape going down between the hedges, the Major upright on the box, and then the bend takes it.

The dinner gong, struck by Fairbrother, and boots in the hall: the Major is back from the town, coat dark with wet, and goes straight in to the master's chair and takes up the carving set as if it had been waiting for him.

nudges.text: Somewhere in the house a clock strikes and is answered by another a half-minute behind it. The light at every window is going.
Lavinia's voice from the back stair, carried down the passage: 'Shall I take the candle up, or will you be locking the study yourself?'

opening.text: Dinner on the second night of the snow, and the master's chair stands empty at the head of the cloth with his place laid as if he might come down. No maid has come up to carry for you: since you answered the Major back in the study doorway with your keys in your fist, Fairbrother has seen to it that the servants' hall sends up its dishes and nothing else, and you serve the table alone from the sideboard. Major Carrington has his gold watch open on the linen beside the empty place and is telling Miss Davenport, loudly enough for the house, that the quarrel was at eleven by it and that he will carry the household's account to the magistrate at the thaw. Mr. Yardley sits white over an untouched plate, and Miss Gresham, who has risen to help with the tureen as no lady should, stands at your elbow with her back to them all.

dining_room.text: The Major's eye finds you each time you pass behind his chair, and stays. He has moved the carving set to his own side of the cloth, where you would have to reach past him for it.
The watch is gone from the cloth. Sleet rattles the north windows and the grate has burned down to a red line nobody has asked you to mend.

The master's chair is empty at the head of the cloth, his place laid, his portrait above the grate looking down the length of the table at the four who are left. The north windows are black and the sleet comes against them in handfuls.

serving_pantry.text: The tray has been stacked and left for you alone; the glass cloths are folded with a valet's precision and not one maid has been near. Fairbrother's message is the empty room.
The plate-warmer ticks as it cools. The lead sink holds one sherry glass, washed and set upside down, that was not among the dinner things you sent up.

interactions.text: You take the weight of the dish and say it low, for her alone: the master kept his settlements at ten, miss, everybody knew it. Her fingers come off the handles. You carry the soup round the table and the table hears nothing but soup; the word she was shaping is never said.
interactions.detail_label: 'Settlements at ten.' carry it round

interactions.text: You lean in over the tureen and ask her outright what she begged the master for at ten. Her face goes to paper. At that moment the yard door bangs and Mr. Yardley is dragged in half-frozen between the groom and Fairbrother, and the first thing he sees is his intended bent to a servant's ear with her back to the room.
interactions.detail_label: 'What did you beg him for, miss?'

interactions.text: You lift the dish from her hands without meeting her eye and go to the Major's place first, as the order of the table requires. Her lips close on whatever they had shaped. The ladle rings once against the rim and she sits down.

You set the dish down beside the open watch and say nothing. The Major closes it with a snap and tells the table that here is a sensible woman who keeps to her plate. Miss Davenport finishes her eleven without a tremor.

You say it to the cloth, not to him: the hall clock struck the half hour through the study door while the voices were still raised, and it was half past ten. Miss Davenport's recital stops in the middle of a word. The Major's hand closes over the watch and stays closed.
interactions.detail_label: 'The hall clock struck half past ten.'

interactions.text: You ask the table's leave and do not wait for it. The long-case clock in the hall stands silent in the cold: Fairbrother has stopped the pendulum for the dead, and the hands are fixed at the hour the body was found this morning. You come back with the chill of the hall on you and nothing in your hands, and the Major is already watching the door. 'The house keeps the hours Fairbrother keeps,' he says.
You say the hour is for the magistrate to fix and not for the housekeeper, and pour his wine. He lets it pass. The watch stays open on the cloth, its chain across the master's plate.
interactions.detail_label: 'That's for the magistrate, sir.'

interactions.text: The glass has been washed by someone who did not wash glasses for a living: a crust of sherry still dried in the foot. On the underside of the rim, where a thumb would not find it, is a single bead of white wax. White wax, in a house where the study candlestick now holds a yellow tallow stub.

With the nephew locked in and Fairbrother set at his door, there is nobody left to send you anywhere. You stack the tray, take up your keys, and go through the service door into the cold of the back passage; behind you the Major's chair scrapes as he rises to see which way you went.

events.text: The Major sets down his glass and tells the table that the quarrel in the study is known to all of them, and that he will carry the household's account to the magistrate at the thaw, name by name and hour by hour. Mr. Yardley kicks his chair over backwards and is out through the yard door into the storm before anyone has risen. The groom and Fairbrother bring him back a quarter of an hour later, white to the lips and his coat stiff with ice, and he is taken up and locked in his room with the valet set on a chair outside it. The chair stays on its back on the carpet.

nudges.text: The Major's voice, pitched to carry through any door in this house: 'The housekeeper will account for her rounds when she has done hiding behind the soup.'
Somewhere above, a door is tried from the inside and found locked, and Fairbrother's chair creaks as he settles against it.

S_T3N02.title: The Hours Go to the Lawyer

opening.text: Grey morning on the stair head, and you have lit one candle against it to walk the night through again, door to door, the rounds book open at half past ten and the single flame at eleven. Reginald Fairbrother stands on the back stair with his own candle, the tallow box square on its shelf behind him, and has not lifted his head to you. On the gallery above, Major Carrington stands at his own door with it open an inch, already asking after your hours. Down in the library, Mr Ellingham waits at the table with the deed box open and has sent up word that the hours come to him first.

stair_head.text: The Major leans on the gallery rail above the newel and asks, civilly enough, whether your hours are written yet and whether he might see them before the lawyer does.
The Major stands at the gallery rail above and says he knows already what a woman who counts clocks has written, and that the magistrate will know what to make of it.

Snow light through the half-landing window, the barometer still falling. Fairbrother's candle on the back stair, the tallow box on its shelf behind him, lid shut. Mrs Ormsby on the half-landing with her hand at the loose side of her hair.

gallery.text: Miss Gresham comes along the Turkey runner as you count doors, gives you a small nod and your surname, and goes down.
Miss Gresham gathers her skirts to the far rail as you count doors, and does not look at your candle.
Three doors, the sconces cold, the waxwings staring from their case. The Major stands at his door, open an inch, and watches you count.

study_end.text: The bare boards below the study keyhole, the fire bucket, the master's bell with its wire slack. The place where the pin lay is a clean inch of dust.
Bare boards here, no runner, and the snow light from the end window lying flat along them to the study door. Something small and black catches your candle an inch below the keyhole.

library.text: Mr Ellingham at the library table with the deed box open and the inkstand drawn to him, a page left clear beneath where your name will go.

interactions.text: 'Eleven,' he says, to the rail, and sets his own candle a half inch straighter upon it. Nothing more, and you write eleven.
interactions.detail_label: 'What hour was the last candle drawn?'

interactions.text: He lifts his head at last. 'The master's hour is mine to speak, and no housekeeper's.' He goes down past you with his candle and the box stays shut behind him.
interactions.detail_label: 'Whom did you light up? Was he alive?'

interactions.text: You lift the lid and count aloud, one short of the dozen, loud enough to carry to Miss Gresham on the landing. She hears the number. Fairbrother shuts the lid over your fingers, not hard, and holds it there.
He goes down without a word. The tallow box stays on its shelf, lid shut, and the hour stays unwritten.
interactions.detail_label: 'Go on down, Mr Fairbrother. Later.'

interactions.text: You put it in her palm and say you found it on the stairs. Her fingers close. 'You are a discreet woman, Mrs—' and your surname, carefully. You let that stand.
You hand it up and say where on the gallery it lay, an inch below the study keyhole. The Major turns it in the snow light. On the half-landing below, Mrs Ormsby goes white to the lips.
You lay it on the page with the place and the hour written beside it. Ellingham folds it into the deed box under his signature with the rest. From the door, Mrs Ormsby watches it go in.
She thanks you and goes past, hand still at her hair. The pin stays in your apron pocket, weighing nothing.
interactions.detail_label: 'Mind the landing, madam. It's dark.'

interactions.text: A jet hairpin, an inch below the study keyhole, where a woman's knee would rest. You know it: you pinned Mrs Ormsby's hair with it for dinner. It lay here before the lamp you saw, or after. It goes into your apron pocket.

He reads your hours through once, door by door, and signs beneath them without a word. When the Major's step comes down the stair behind you he closes the deed box and says, 'They go to the magistrate, Major. Not before.'
interactions.detail_label: 'Put your name under mine, sir.'

events.text: The roof lets go its snow: it slides past every gallery window in one grey mass and lands below with a sound like a door shut on the whole house. The Major's door opens wide.

nudges.text: The Major's voice, carrying down the stairwell: 'The housekeeper's hours, Ellingham. I'll have them before any lawyer does.'
From below, the dry snap of a deed-box clasp. Mr Ellingham is waiting, and a solicitor's patience is counted by the hour.

opening.text: The eaves have begun to drip, and the lodge-keeper has waded up to say the road will carry a cart by noon. Major Carrington has ordered the carriage, barred you from the first floor, and sent Lavinia Netherby up to the study grate with pails, a fresh scuttle and the ash sieve; Mr Ellingham has gone up after her and called the maids down in law's name, and from the gallery rail his voice and the Major's cross above your head. Wet coal drips from the hod on the landing; Lavinia has not come down, and the Major's step is on the main stair behind you.

stair_head.text: The hall chair is set square across your door, and the key is on your side of the lock. Fairbrother has left it there and is looking at the half-landing window as if he had not.
The hall chair is set square across your door. The key has been turned from his side, and he holds it in the hand that is not holding the candle.
At the foot of the stairs Lavinia has your candle ready, unlit, held out in red hands before you ask for it.
At the foot of the stairs Lavinia stands with your candle unlit and looks from the Major's door to the lawyer's to the valet's chair; she waits for Fairbrother's nod before she lifts it.
Grey snow light through the half-landing window. Wet coal drips from the hod set down on the stair-rods, the sieve beside it, and the barometer has begun, for the first time in three days, to rise.

library.text: Breakfast was laid here, the dining room being cold; Mrs Ormsby's cup stands by the doctor's, and she praised the housekeeping to him across you, loudly enough for the Major.
Breakfast was laid here, the dining room being cold. Mrs Ormsby took her tea in her room and sent the tray down untouched; it stands on the library table still.
The deed box is open on the library table, the inkstand filled, the wax jack lit. The papers lie squared for signing, and the master's reading chair has been turned to the wall.

gallery.text: The Major's door stands open so that the gallery may be watched from inside it. Mr Ellingham waits on the Turkey runner with his hat in his hand, as a man waits who has said a thing in law's name and means to be seen having said it.

Pails stand along the Turkey runner where the maids set them down and left. Mr Ellingham waits by the case of waxwings; the widow's door is shut, and the snow light through the gallery windows has gone the colour of dishwater.

study_end.text: The study door is shut again and the bare boards swept. Whatever was in the grate is in the grate no longer, or in an apron, or down the back stairs.
The study door stands open for the first time since the night. Lavinia kneels at the dead grate with the sieve, the fire bucket beside her, and grey ash sifts through a trembling mesh.

interactions.text: You put her out by the back way and kneel to the grate yourself. Under the ash is a curl of paper that was not coal, and it is in your apron, or very nearly, when the step reaches the door: either the Major finds the grate raked clean and you on your feet, or Ellingham finds you kneeling with your hands black and has you out of the study in law's name.
interactions.detail_label: send her down; rake the grate yourself

interactions.text: You leave her the sieve and go down to Mr Ellingham. Behind you the Major comes in and finds the girl alone at the grate with ash on her apron, and she does not know whose order to give him.
interactions.detail_label: leave her at the grate; go to Ellingham

interactions.text: You stand in the door and say it. The Major looks past you at the girl, and the girl goes down the stair with her apron held shut in both hands.
interactions.detail_label: 'She found nothing, sir.'

interactions.text: She breathes. The sieve steadies a little, and the ash goes on falling through it, and the step goes on coming up the stair.
interactions.detail_label: 'Steady the sieve. Breathe.'

interactions.text: You open the door, set the cup on the boards beside his chair, and go back in. He drinks it. An hour later he says, to the wall and not to the door, that the master was warm at eleven.
He sets the cup down untouched. Forty years, he says, has outlasted heirs before, and he does not look at you when he says it.
interactions.detail_label: 'The heir will ask who sat guard.'

interactions.text: The passage is black and smells of lavender and cold plaster. Either the press gives and you are on the study end in grey light with your eye to the keyhole, or it is locked from the gallery side and you come back to find Fairbrother has turned his chair to face the linen press and not your door.
interactions.detail_label: slip through the linen press passage

interactions.text: 'It is wax, Mrs. It is enough.' He does not move the chair.
interactions.detail_label: 'Is the candle enough?'

interactions.text: The colour comes off the rim in the cold water and goes grey in the ewer. When the Major's man comes to turn the room over it is one of twelve on the tray, and you have nothing to say of ten o'clock.
interactions.detail_label: wash it; back among the dozen

interactions.text: Lavinia goes up with the message and comes down without one. Millicent Gresham comes down herself a quarter-hour after, white to the lips, and asks you at the door what you want for it.
interactions.detail_label: send Lavinia to Miss Gresham

interactions.text: You lay the book over it again and shut the drawer. The water stands in the ewer and Lavinia goes on down the stair.
interactions.detail_label: leave it under the account book

interactions.text: He nods, which is his habit, and says the widow has asked after the housekeeping, and goes to his own door.
interactions.detail_label: 'Under the back stairs; I didn't look.'

interactions.text: He says nothing, which is also his habit. The snow runs off his boots onto the flags, and he goes along the gallery to her door instead of his own.
interactions.detail_label: 'Outside Mrs Ormsby's door, sir.'

interactions.text: 'I will,' he says, and does not go to fetch them, and does not take his eyes off your face.
interactions.detail_label: 'You will want dry boots, Doctor.'

interactions.text: Going down with the ewer you pass Lavinia's door ajar. In her tin candlestick is a yellow tallow stub burned flat to the socket. The maids burn tallow; the study burns wax. A tallow stub among the study's wax would mean nothing of the maids, and everything of who carried a maid's candle upstairs.
interactions.detail_label: carry the ewer down the maids' stair

interactions.text: You go down the main stair with your hands folded, past the wet hod and the sieve, to where the house is assembling to hear what the housekeeper saw.
interactions.detail_label: down to the drawing room, to give account

events.text: Mr Ellingham comes down from the gallery and, passing you on the stair, names his price without lowering his voice: the unsigned will never passes your lips. The Major sets Fairbrother on the hall chair square across your door, takes Dr Ashcombe by the elbow, and walks him across the slush to the ice house himself.

Wheels in the slush below: the carriage is brought round. The Major's voice carries up the well of the stair: the house will assemble in the drawing room to hear the housekeeper's account of the night, and then the papers will be signed.

nudges.text: The Major's voice, from somewhere below: 'Noon, Ellingham. The road carries a cart at noon, and I will have her account before it.'
The drip from the eaves has found the coal hod and rings on wet coal, slow as a clock.

opening.text: The whole house is gathered at the study end, and the Major has your rounds book open on the linen press with Mr Ellingham's pen laid across it. 'You will sign it,' he says. 'Eleven o'clock, the lamp through the keyhole, and your name beneath, or say before these people that you cannot.' The master's key hangs on his waistcoat chain, bow turned to the sconces; Mr Yardley stands at your elbow, Dr Ashcombe at the widow's, and the study door is still locked between you all and what the lamp showed. Fairbrother's candle burns at the stair head, and in two days no one has asked him his hour.

study_end.text: The master's key stands in the study lock, bow outward, and the keyhole is dark. The Major's shoulders are still held; nobody has told Mr Yardley he may let go.
Miss Gresham stands at Nathaniel's side, not behind him, and meets your eye once, steadily, before she looks back to the Major.
Miss Gresham keeps Nathaniel's arm between herself and you and does not look up from the Turkey runner.
Mrs Ormsby has come nearest the study door of any of them, her hands folded, ready to be asked to look.
Mrs Ormsby keeps to the end window, with Dr Ashcombe's shoulder set between her and you.
Bare boards, the fire bucket, the linen press with your rounds book open on it. The study door is locked, and the whole house is breathing in the one cold corridor.

stair_head.text: Fairbrother has left the newel post and stands a pace behind your shoulder, candle shielded in his palm, as a valet stands behind a master.
Fairbrother has gone down to the foot of the stairs with his candle and stands there with his head down, as if waiting to be sent for.
Fairbrother waits at the newel post with his candle, the grey snow light from the half-landing window on his back.

interactions.text: You give it as you would give the week's accounts. A key in the inside lock fills the keyhole; at midnight you saw lamplight through it, so no key stood there. The tallow stub lies on the bare boards where no wax belongs, because a man waited in the dark outside this door. Ellingham writes it. No servant's hour goes down on his page, and at the stair head Fairbrother's head comes up for the first time in two days.
interactions.detail_label: 'The key, the lamp, the stub. No more.'

interactions.text: You say the key and the lamp and the stub, and then you add the rest: that at eleven Fairbrother lit a gentleman up the back stairs, and knows whose coat it was. Every face on the gallery turns from the Major to the stair head. The valet's candle shakes. He must answer now, before the Major's own hour is written, and he knows it.
interactions.detail_label: 'Fairbrother lit a man up at eleven.'

interactions.text: 'Eleven, Major. By your own watch, which you held to the sconce while you told me the hour.' You read him his night back, step by step, before the whole house: the gallery, the dark, the stub, the key in his pocket when he came to say the door was locked. He stops fighting Nathaniel's grip and looks at you, not with anger: as at a thing to be remembered.
interactions.detail_label: 'Eleven, Major. By your own watch.'

interactions.text: Nathaniel shifts his grip and the Major's breath whistles through his teeth. Ellingham waits with his pen lifted. Nothing has yet been said that can be written down.
interactions.detail_label: 'Hold him, Mr Yardley. Mind his arm.'

interactions.text: 'A key standing in the inside lock fills the keyhole, sir. At midnight I saw the lamp through it.' You step to him, lift the master's key off his chain before his hand can close, and set it in the study lock from this side, bow outward. 'Look.' Ellingham kneels, then the doctor, then the widow; the keyhole is black. The Major's open hand catches your cheek and the sconces jump. Nathaniel Yardley has his arms pinned behind him before the second blow, and you name him there, the tallow stub on the boards behind his heel. Fairbrother, at the stair head, has never once been asked his hour.

Ellingham closes the rounds book over his pen. 'The drawing room, I think, and a fair copy. Mr Yardley, bring him.' The house goes down the stairs in the order it came up, and you go last, as staff do, past Fairbrother's candle.

The Major, raised, from wherever he stands: 'Sign it, woman, or say before them all that you cannot.'

opening.text: The thaw has come overnight and the house drips at every gutter. On the deal desk lie your wages counted out in coin and a character in Mr Yardley's hand, which says that a woman who put her hand in a gentleman's pocket cannot be kept; Lavinia Netherby is roping your box by the stove and will not look up. Through the barred window the carriage stands on the gravel with Major Carrington and Mr Ellingham already inside it, the study key and the tallow stub gone with them, the unsigned will never once named. Overhead, in the front hall, Mr Yardley is handing the house keys to Reginald Fairbrother.
